Brendan Edward Hassett is an American mathematician who is a professor of mathematics at [Brown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_University).
Bridgeland stability condition is an algebro-geometric stability condition defined on elements of a [triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category).

Brieskorn–Grothendieck resolution is a resolution conjectured by [Alexander Grothendieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grothendieck), that in particular gives a resolution of the universal deformation of a [Kleinian singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleinian_singularity).

Brill–Noether theory, introduced by , is the study of special divisors, certain [divisors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor_on_an_algebraic_curve) on a [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) that determine more compatible functions than would be predicted.

Brouwer's conjecture is a conjecture by [Andries Brouwer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andries_Brouwer) on upper bounds for the intermediate sums of the [eigenvalues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors) of the [Laplacian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplacian_matrix) of a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) in term of its number of edges.

Brown–Gitler spectrum is a [spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_(topology)) whose [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology) is a certain [cyclic module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_module) over the [Steenrod algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steenrod_algebra).

Brumer–Stark conjecture is a [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) in [algebraic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_theory) giving a rough generalization of both the [analytic class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_class_number_formula) for [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function)s, and also of [Stickelberger's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stickelberger's_theorem) about the [factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorization) of [Gauss sums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sums).
Bryan Lynn Shader (born 17 December 1961) is a professor of mathematics at the [University of Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wyoming).

Budan's theorem is a theorem for bounding the number of real roots of a polynomial in an interval, and computing the [parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)) of this number.

Buekenhout geometry or diagram geometry is a generalization of [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space)s, [Tits building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tits_building)s, and several other geometric structures, introduced by .

building (also Tits building, named after [Jacques Tits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Tits)) is a combinatorial and geometric structure which simultaneously generalizes certain aspects of [flag manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_manifold)s, finite [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane)s, and [Riemannian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_symmetric_space)s.

Bumblebee models are effective field theories describing a vector field with a [vacuum expectation value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_expectation_value) that spontaneously breaks Lorentz symmetry.

[Algebraic combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_combinatorics) is an area of [Combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics).

Algebraic number theory is both the study of [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) by [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra)ic methods and the theory of [algebraic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number)s.

algebraic structure consists of one or more [sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closure_(mathematics)) under one or more [operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_(mathematics)), satisfying some [axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom).

Algebraic topology is a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) in which tools from [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra) are used to study [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s.
anomaly is a breaking of a symmetry which exists at the classical level.

[Bialgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bialgebra) In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), a bialgebra over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K is a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) over K which is both a [unital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unital_algebra) [associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) and a [coalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalgebra), such that these structures are compatible.
Category theory is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) theory that deals in an abstract way with mathematical structures and relationships between them.

commutative algebra is the area of [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra) dealing with [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring)s and commutative [modules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) and [algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) over commutative rings.

definition: [computer algebra system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_algebra_system) (CAS) or symbolic computation system is a system of software packages that facilitates [symbolic mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbolic_mathematics).
diagram algebra is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) in which operations are performed using diagrams rather than traditional techniques.
Differential algebra is the formal, algebraic study of the processes of [differential calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_calculus).
Electromagnetism is the set of phenomena associated with [electricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity) and [magnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetism).

Elementary algebra is a fundamental and relatively basic form of [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra) taught to students who are presumed to have little or no formal knowledge of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) beyond [arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic).
Field theory is a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) which studies the properties of [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics))s.
Galois theory is a branch of [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra).
General relativity is the best known relativistic [classical field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_field_theory) of [gravitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitation).
geometric group theory is the study of groups by geometric methods.
Gravity is the equilibrium of energy expressed by and shared between two or more objects of mass in space.

[group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) is a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)), together with a [binary operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation) satisfying certain axioms, detailed in the group article.

Homological algebra is a collection of [algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra) techniques that originated in the study of [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) but has also found applications to [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory) and [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).
Homotopical algebra is a vast generalization of [homological algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_algebra) to non-linear objects such as commutative rings, and spectra.
homotopy theory is the study of [homotopy groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_groups); and more generally of the category of topological spaces and homotopy classes of continuous mappings.

isomorphism theorems consist of three (or sometimes four) [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem)s describing the structure of [homomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homomorphism)s of many different types of [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure)s.

Knot theory is a branch of [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) that concerns itself with abstract properties of [mathematical knots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_(mathematics)) the spatial arrangements that in principle could be assumed by a closed loop of string.

Linear algebra is the branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) concerned with the study of [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector)s, [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s (also called linear spaces), [linear map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map)s (also called linear transformations), and [systems of linear equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_linear_equations).
Matrix theory is a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) that focuses on the study of [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)).

Moduli theory is a branch of the fields of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold)s and [singularity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_theory).

Moonshine theory is a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) that deals with the connections between [finite simple group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups)s and [modular function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_function)s etc.

Numerical linear algebra is the intersection of [numerical analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_analysis) and [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra): its purpose is the design and analysis of [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm)s for the numerical solution of [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) problems.
octonions are a [nonassociative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonassociative) extension of the [quaternion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion)s.

parastatistics is one of several alternatives to the better known [particle statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_statistics) models ([Bose–Einstein statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bose–Einstein_statistics), [Fermi–Dirac statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi–Dirac_statistics) and [Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell–Boltzmann_statistics)).
Process calculi (or process algebras) are a diverse family of related approaches to formally modelling [concurrent system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concurrent_system)s.

quaternions are a non-commutative extension of the [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number)s which have numerous applications in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics), and [computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_graphics).

[rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number)s, that is, those [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)s which can be represented in the form: is not equal to [zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/0_(number)).

ring theory is the study of [rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics))—[algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure)s in which addition and multiplication are defined and have similar properties to those familiar from the [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)s.

Scattering theory is the theory of scattering events which can occur as well in [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics), classical [electrodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrodynamics) or [acoustics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustics).
sedenions are a [nonassociative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonassociative) extension of the [octonions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octonions).

String theory is a branch of [theoretical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_physics) that attempts to build a theory of [quantum gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_gravity) using one-dimensional strings rather than zero-dimensional point particles as fundamental building blocks.
Super linear algebra is a generalization of [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra) to include a Z -gradation on all objects.
[tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor) is a certain kind of geometrical entity and [array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) concept.

[topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group) G is a group that is also a topological space such that the group multiplication G × G→G and the inverse operation G→G are continuous maps.

toric section is a [plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_curve) that results from the intersection of a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)) with a [torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torus).
causal fermion systems is an approach to describe [fundamental physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_physics).

Cayley surface, named after [Arthur Cayley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Cayley), is a [cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_surface) [nodal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nodal_surface) in 3-dimensional [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) with four conical points.

Cayleyan is a [variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) associated to a [hypersurface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersurface) by , who named it the pippian in and also called it the Steiner–Hessian.

cellular algebra is a [finite-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite-dimensional) [associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) A with a distinguished cellular basis which is particularly well-adapted to studying the [representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory) of A.

center or centre is used in various contexts in [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra) to denote the set of all those elements that [commute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_operation) with all other elements.
center of a ring is the [subring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subring) consisting of the elements such that for all elements in .
central carrier of a projection E is the smallest central projection, in the von Neumann algebra, that dominates E.
central charge is an [operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_(mathematics)) Z that [commutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutativity) with all the other symmetry operators.

central polynomial for n-by-n [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) is a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) in non-commuting variables that is non-constant but yields a scalar matrix whenever it is evaluated at n-by-n matrices.

central series is a kind of [normal series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_series) of [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup)s or [Lie subalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_subalgebra)s, expressing the idea that the [[Commutator#Group theory|commutator]] is nearly trivial.

central simple algebra (CSA) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K is a finite-dimensional [associative K-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) A that is [simple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_algebra), and for which the [center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_(ring_theory)) is exactly K.
centrosymmetric matrix is a [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) which is symmetric about its center.
CH-quasigroup, introduced by , is a symmetric [quasigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasigroup) in which any three elements generate an abelian quasigroup.

Chaff is an [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) for solving instances of the [Boolean satisfiability problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_satisfiability_problem) in programming.

chain is a [formal linear combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_linear_combination) of the [-cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-cell_(mathematics)) in a [cell complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CW_complex).

chain complex is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) that consists of a sequence of [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group)s (or [modules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics))) and a sequence of [homomorphisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_homomorphism) between consecutive groups such that the [image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_(mathematics)) of each homomorphism is contained in the [[kernel (algebra)#Group homomorphisms|kernel]] of the next.
change of fiber is a map between the fibers induced by paths in B.
change of rings is an operation of changing a coefficient ring to another.

change of variables is a basic technique used to simplify problems in which the original [variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_(mathematics))s are replaced with [functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) of other variables.

character group is the [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) of [representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_representation)s of an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group) by [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number)-valued [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics))s.

character table is a two-dimensional table whose rows correspond to [irreducible representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreducible_representation)s, and whose columns correspond to [conjugacy class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugacy_class)es of [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) elements.

definition: characteristic of a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) , often denoted , is defined to be the smallest positive number of copies of the ring's [multiplicative identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_element) () that will sum to the [additive identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additive_identity) ().

characteristic polynomial of a [square matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_matrix) is a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) which is [invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_(mathematics)) under [matrix similarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_similarity) and has the [eigenvalues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues) as [roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_polynomial).

characteristic variety of a [microdifferential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microdifferential_operator) P is an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) that is the zero set of the [principal symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_symbol) of P in the [cotangent bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotangent_bundle).

definition: Chebotarev theorem on roots of unity was originally a conjecture made by [Ostrowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Ostrowski) in the context of [lacunary series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacunary_function).

Chebyshev iteration is an [[Iterative method#Linear systems|iterative method]] for determining the solutions of a [system of linear equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_linear_equations).
Chern–Simons forms are certain secondary [characteristic class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_class)es.

Chern–Simons theory is a 3-dimensional [topological quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_quantum_field_theory) of [[Topological quantum field theory#Schwarz-type TQFTs|Schwarz type]].

Chevalley basis for a [simple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Lie_group) [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) is a [basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_(linear_algebra)) constructed by [Claude Chevalley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Chevalley) with the property that all [[Algebra over a field#Structure coefficients|structure constants]] are integers.

Chevalley restriction theorem describes functions on a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) which are invariant under the [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action) of a Lie group in terms of functions on a [Cartan subalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan_subalgebra).

Chevalley–Iwahori–Nagata theorem states that if a [linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group) G is [acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) linearly on a finite-dimensional [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) V, then the map from V/G to the [spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_ring) of the ring of [invariant polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_theory) is an [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_isomorphism) if this ring is finitely generated and all [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) of G on V are [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_set) .

chiral algebra is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) introduced by Beilinson and Drinfeld (2004) of [translations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_(geometry)).

chiral Lie algebra is a [D-module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-module) on a curve with a certain structure of [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra).

Chiral magnetic effect (CME) is the generation of [electric current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_current) along an external [magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_field) induced by [chirality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirality) imbalance.

definition: chiral Potts curve is an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) defined over the [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number)s that occurs in the study of the [chiral Potts model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_Potts_model) of [statistical mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics).

chiral symmetry breaking generally refers to the dynamical spontaneous breaking of a [chiral symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_symmetry) associated with massless [fermions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermion).

Chow groups (named after [Wei-Liang Chow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wei-Liang_Chow) by ) of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) over any [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) are algebro-geometric analogs of the [homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_(mathematics)) of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space).

Chow variety is an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) whose points correspond to effective [algebraic cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycles) of fixed dimension and degree on a given [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space).
Chow's lemma, named after [Wei-Liang Chow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wei-Liang_Chow), is one of the foundational results in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

Chow's moving lemma, proved by , states: given [algebraic cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycles) Y, Z on a [nonsingular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_variety) [quasi-projective variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-projective_variety) X, there is another algebraic cycle Z' which is [rationally equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationally_equivalent) to Z on X, such that Y and Z' intersect properly.

circular ensembles are measures on spaces of [unitary matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_matrix) introduced by [Freeman Dyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeman_Dyson) as modifications of the [Gaussian matrix ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_matrix_ensemble)s.
cissoid (; ) is a [plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_curve) generated from two given curves , and a point (the pole).
class formation is a topological group acting on a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) satisfying certain conditions.

class function is a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) on a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) G that is constant on the [conjugacy class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugacy_class)es of G.

classical groups are the matrix groups arising from finite-dimensional vector spaces and from [nondegenerate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nondegenerate_form) [bilinear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilinear_form), [sesquilinear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesquilinear_form), [quadratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form), and [Hermitian form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_form)s.

definition: classifying space BG of a [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group) G is the quotient of a [weakly contractible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_contractible) space EG (i.e., a topological space all of whose [homotopy group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_group)s are trivial) by a proper [free action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_action) of G.

clean ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) in which every element can be written as the sum of a [unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_(ring_theory)) and an [idempotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotent_element_(ring_theory)).

clearing denominators, also called clearing fractions, is a technique for simplifying an [equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation) equating two expressions that each are a sum of [rational expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_function)s – which includes simple [fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraction_(mathematics))s.

Clebsch diagonal cubic surface, or Klein's icosahedral cubic surface, is a non-singular [cubic surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_surface), studied by and , all of whose 27 [exceptional line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exceptional_line)s can be defined over the real numbers.

Clifford algebra is an [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) generated by a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) with a [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form), and is a [unital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unital_algebra) [associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) with the additional structure of a distinguished subspace.

Clifford bundle is an [algebra bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_bundle) whose fibers have the structure of a [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra) and whose [local trivialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_trivialization)s respect the algebra structure.
Clifford module is a [representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_of_an_algebra) of a [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra).

Clifford module bundle, a bundle of Clifford modules or just Clifford module is a [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) whose fibers are [Clifford module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_module)s, the representations of [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra)s.

Clifford's theorem on special divisors is a result of on [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve)s, showing the constraints on [special linear system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_linear_system)s on a curve C.

CN-groups, groups in which the centralizer of a non-identity element is [nilpotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilpotent_group), of odd order are solvable .

cocycle category of objects X, Y in a [model category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_category) is a [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) in which the objects are pairs of maps is [bijective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijective).

codimension is a basic [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) idea that applies to [subspaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_subspace) in [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s, to [submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold)s in [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s, and suitable [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset)s of [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_varieties).

coefficient is a [multiplicative factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factor_(arithmetic)) involved in some [term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summand) of a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial), a [series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Series_(mathematics)), or any other type of [expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expression_(mathematics)).

coefficient matrix is a [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) consisting of the [coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient)s of the variables in a set of [linear equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_equations).

Cohen algebra, named after [Paul Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Cohen_(mathematician)), is a type of [Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_(structure)) used in the theory of [forcing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forcing_(mathematics)).
Cohen ring is a field or a complete [discrete valuation ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_valuation_ring) of [mixed characteristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_characteristic) .

Cohen structure theorem, introduced by , describes the structure of [complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_(ring_theory)) [Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) [local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring)s.

Cohen–Macaulay ring is a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) with some of the [algebro-geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) properties of a [smooth variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_variety), such as local [equidimensionality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidimensionality).

coherent algebra is an [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) of complex square matrices that is closed under [ordinary matrix multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_multiplication), [Schur product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_product_(matrices)), [transposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_transpose), and contains both the [identity matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_matrix) [[Category:Algebras]] [[Category:Algebraic combinatorics]] cixny10baaqyddcy8sdlg4rqeyorfyi

coherent duality is any of a number of generalisations of [Serre duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre_duality), applying to [coherent sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaves), in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold) theory, as well as some aspects of [commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra) that are part of the 'local' theory.

coherent ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) in which every [[Ideal_(ring_theory)#Types_of_ideals|finitely generated]] left [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) is [finitely presented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_presented_module).

determinantal varieties are spaces of matrices with a given upper bound on their [rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank_(linear_algebra))s.

differential algebraic group is a [differential algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebraic_variety) with a compatible [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) structure.

differential Galois theory is the field that studies extensions of [differential field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_field)s.

direct integral or Hilbert integral is a generalization of the concept of a [direct sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_sum).
direct limit is a way to construct a (typically large) object from many (typically smaller) objects that are put together in a specific way.
direct limit of groups is the [direct limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_limit) of a direct system of [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)).

direct sum of two [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) is the [diagonal matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal_matrix) where the top-left and bottom-right corners of the matrix fill the two given matrices, and where the top-right and bottom-left corners are all [zeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeros).

directed algebraic topology is a refinement of [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) for directed spaces, [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s and their [combinatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics) counterparts equipped with some notion of direction.

doomsday conjecture was a conjecture about [Ext group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ext_group)s over the [Steenrod algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steenrod_algebra) made by Joel Cohen, named by Michael Barratt, published by and disproved by .

double coset is a collection of [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) elements which are equivalent under the symmetries coming from two [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup)s, generalizing the notion of a single [coset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coset).
double group was introduced by [Hans Bethe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Bethe) for the quantitative treatment of [magnetochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetochemistry).

dressed particle or clothed particle is a [bare particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bare_particle) together with some excitations of other [quantum field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field)s that are inseparable from the bare particle.

Drinfeld module (or elliptic module) is roughly a special kind of [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) over a ring of functions on a curve over a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field), generalizing the Carlitz module.

de Sitter/conformal field theory correspondence, shortened to dS/CFT correspondence, is a [de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Sitter_space) analogue of the [anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space) version known as [adS/CFT correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AdS/CFT_correspondence).
Du Bois singularities are singularities of [complex varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_algebraic_variety) studied by Du Bois.

Du Val singularity, also called simple surface singularity, Kleinian singularity, or rational double point, is an isolated singularity of a complex surface which is modeled on a double branched cover of the plane, with minimal resolution obtained by replacing the singular point with a tree of smooth rational curves, with intersection pattern dual to a Dynkin diagram of [A-D-E singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADE_classification) type.

definition: dual graph of a [planar graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planar_graph) is a graph that has a [vertex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(graph_theory)) for each [face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_(graph_theory)) of .

dual norm is a measure of size for a [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function) [linear function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_function) defined on a [normed vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normed_vector_space).
dual numbers are a [quadratic algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_algebra) first introduced in the 19th century.

dualizing module, also called a canonical module, is a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) over a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) that is analogous to the [canonical bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_bundle) of a [smooth variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_variety).

dualizing sheaf on a [proper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_scheme) [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) X of dimension n over a field k is a [coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf) to construct the dualizing sheaf on X.

Duflo isomorphism is an [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) between the center of the [universal enveloping algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_enveloping_algebra) of a finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) over a [[Characteristic_0#Fields_of_characteristic_zero|field of characteristic zero]] and the invariants of its [symmetric algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_algebra).

Dwork family is a one-parameter family of [hypersurface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersurface)s depending on an integer n, studied by [Bernard Dwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Dwork).

Dynkin diagram, named for [Eugene Dynkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Dynkin), is a type of [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) with some edges doubled or tripled (drawn as a double or triple line).

Dyson conjecture is a [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) about the constant term of certain [Laurent polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_polynomial)s, [proved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_proof) independently in 1962 by [[Kenneth G.

Dyson series, formulated by [Freeman Dyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeman_Dyson), is a [perturbative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perturbation_theory_(quantum_mechanics)) expansion of the [time evolution operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_evolution_operator) in the [interaction picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interaction_picture).

dévissage is a technique introduced by [Alexander Grothendieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grothendieck) for proving statements about [coherent sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf) on [Noetherian scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_scheme)s.

E-dense semigroup (also called an E-inversive semigroup) is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) in which every element a has at least one [weak inverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_inverse) x, meaning that xax = x.
E-functions are a type of [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series) that satisfy particular arithmetic conditions on the coefficients.

E-semigroup is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) in which the [idempotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotent)s form a [subsemigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsemigroup).
Early Algebra is an approach to early [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) teaching and learning.

Eckmann–Hilton argument (or Eckmann–Hilton principle or Eckmann–Hilton theorem) is an [argument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument) about two [unital magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unital_magma) structures on a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) where one is a [homomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homomorphism) for the other.

edge space and vertex space of an [undirected graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undirected_graph) are [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s defined in terms of the [edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(graph_theory)) and [vertex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(graph_theory)) sets, respectively.

edge-transitive graph is a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) such that, given any two edges and of , there is an [automorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_automorphism) of that [maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Map_(mathematics)) to .

Eduardo Casas-Alvero (born 1948) is a Spanish [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) and a professor at the [University of Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Barcelona).

Effect algebras are [partial algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_algebra) which abstract the (partial) algebraic properties of events that can be observed in [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics).

quantum effective action is a modified expression for the [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_physics) [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_(physics)) taking into account quantum corrections while ensuring that the [principle of least action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_action) applies, meaning that extremizing the effective action yields the [equations of motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equations_of_motion) for the [vacuum expectation values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_expectation_value) of the quantum fields.

effective field theory is a type of approximation, or [effective theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_theory), for an underlying physical theory, such as a [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) or a [statistical mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics) model.

Egbert Valentin Brieskorn (7 July 1936 in [Rostock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rostock) – 11 July 2013 in [Bonn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonn)) was a German mathematician who introduced [Brieskorn sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brieskorn_sphere)s and the [Brieskorn–Grothendieck resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brieskorn–Grothendieck_resolution).

Egyptian algebra, as that term is used in this article, refers to [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra) as it was developed and used in [ancient Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt).

Ehlers group, named after [Jürgen Ehlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jürgen_Ehlers), is a finite-dimensional transformation group of stationary [vacuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum) [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime)s which maps solutions of [Einstein's field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein's_field_equations) to other solutions.

eigengap of a [linear operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_operator) is the difference between two successive [eigenvalues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues), where eigenvalues are sorted in ascending order.

eigenplane is a two-dimensional [invariant subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace) in a given [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space).
eigenvalue perturbation problem is that of finding the [eigenvectors and eigenvalues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvector) of a system Rabinowitz, P.

eigenvector ( ) or characteristic vector is a (nonzero) [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_(mathematics_and_physics)) that has its [direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direction_(geometry)) unchanged (or reversed) by a given [linear transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map).

definition: Einstein notation (also known as the Einstein summation convention or Einstein summation notation) is a notational convention that implies [summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summation) over a set of indexed terms in a formula, thus achieving brevity.
Eisenstein sum is a finite sum depending on a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field) and related to a [Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum).

Electronic Journal of Linear Algebra is a [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [platinum open access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_open_access) [scientific journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_journal) covering [matrix analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_analysis) and [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra), together with their applications.

elementary abelian group is an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group) in which all elements other than the identity have the same [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(group_theory)).

elementary function is a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) of a single [variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_(mathematics)) ([real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_a_real_variable) or [[Complex analysis#Complex functions|complex]]) that is typically encountered by beginners.

elementary matrix is a square [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) obtained from the application of a single elementary row operation to the [identity matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_matrix).
elementary number is one formalization of the concept of a [closed-form number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed-form_number).

elementary particle or fundamental particle is a [New York}} == External links == The most important address about the current experimental and theoretical knowledge about elementary particle physics is the [[Particle Data Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York}}_==_External_links_==_The_most_important_address_about_the_current_experimental_and_theoretical_knowledge_about_elementary_particle_physics_is_the_[[Particle_Data_Group), where different international institutions collect all experimental data and give short reviews over the contemporary theoretical understanding.

eleven-dimensional supergravity is the theory of [supergravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergravity) in the highest number of [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s allowed for a supersymmetric theory.

elimination theory is the classical name for algorithmic approaches to eliminating some variables between [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s of several variables, in order to solve [systems of polynomial equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_of_polynomial_equations).

Elitzur's theorem states that in [gauge theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory), the only operators that can have non-vanishing [expectation values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_expectation_value) are ones that are invariant under local gauge transformations.

elliptic algebra is a certain [regular algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_algebra) of a [Gelfand–Kirillov dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand–Kirillov_dimension) three ([quantum polynomial ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_polynomial_ring) in three variables) that corresponds to a cubic divisor in the projective space P .
elliptic Gauss sum is an analog of a [Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum) depending on an [elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve) with complex multiplication.

elliptic singularity of a surface, introduced by Philip Wagreich in 1970, is a surface singularity such that the [arithmetic genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_genus) of its [local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring) is ==See also== *[Rational singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_singularity) ==References== [[Category:Algebraic surfaces]] [[Category:Singularity theory]] ll6vmakxlyz8norxrw0zfv53h1ynr0k

elliptic surface is a surface that has an elliptic [fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration), in other words a [proper morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_morphism) with connected [fibers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_(mathematics)) to an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) such that almost all fibers are [smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_scheme) curves of [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus_(mathematics)) 1.

elliptic units are certain units of [abelian extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_extension)s of [imaginary quadratic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_quadratic_field)s constructed using singular values of [modular function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_function)s, or division values of [elliptic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_function)s.

ELSV formula, named after its four authors , , [Michael Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shapiro_(mathematician)), [Alek Vainshtein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alek_Vainshtein), is an equality between a Hurwitz number (counting [ramified covering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramified_covering)s of the sphere) and an integral over the [moduli space of stable curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_algebraic_curves).
embedding (or imbedding consists of the embeddings in the previous sense.
embedding problem is a generalization of the [inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem).

semigroup with no elements (the empty semigroup) is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) in which the [underlying set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underlying_set) is the [empty set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empty_set).
Endrass surface is a [nodal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nodal_surface) of degree 8 with 168 real nodes, found by .

Engel identity, named after [Friedrich Engel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engel_(mathematician)), is a mathematical equation that is satisfied by all elements of a [Lie ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_ring), in the case of an Engel Lie ring, or by all the elements of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)), in the case of an [Engel group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engel_group).
Engel subalgebra of a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) with respect to some element x is the subalgebra of elements annihilated by some power of ad x.
Enneper surface is a self-intersecting surface that can be described [parametrically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameter) by: for higher order algebraic Enneper surfaces.

Enriques surfaces are [algebraic surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_surface)s such that the irregularity q = 0 and the [canonical line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_line_bundle) K is non-trivial but has trivial square.
Enriques–Babbage theorem states that a [canonical curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_curve) is either a set-theoretic intersection of quadrics, or trigonal, or a plane quintic.

entanglement-assisted stabilizer formalism is a method for protecting quantum information with the help of entanglement shared between a sender and receiver before they transmit quantum data over a quantum communication channel.

enumerative geometry is the branch of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) concerned with counting numbers of solutions to geometric questions, mainly by means of [intersection theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_theory).

enveloping von Neumann algebra of a [C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebra) is a [von Neumann algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_algebra) that, in some sense, contains all the operator-algebraic information about the given C*-algebra.
epigroup is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) in which every element has a power that belongs to a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup).

equating the coefficients is a way of solving a functional equation of two expressions such as [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s for a number of unknown [parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameter)s.
equisingularity is, roughly, a family of singularities that are not non-equivalent and is an important notion in [singularity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_theory).

equitable partition of the vertex set V of a graph G = (V, E) is a [partition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_a_set) of V such that, for any pair of vertices u and v in the same set of the partition and any set B of the partition, both u and v have the same number of neighbors in B.

equivariant cohomology (or Borel cohomology) is a [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory) from [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) which applies to [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s with a [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)).

equivariant Artin L-function is a function associated to a finite [Galois extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_extension) of [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field)s created by packaging together the various [Artin L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_L-function)s associated with the extension.

Erdős–Diophantine graph is an object in the [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) subject of [Diophantine equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_equations) consisting of a set of [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) points at integer distances in the plane that cannot be extended by any additional points.

Erlangen program is a method of characterizing [geometries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) based on [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory) and [projective geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_geometry).

essential dimension is an [invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_(mathematics)) defined for certain [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure)s such as [algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_group)s and [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form)s.
essential manifold is a special type of closed manifold.
essential subgroup is a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) that determines much of the structure of its containing group.

Euclidean domain (also called a Euclidean ring) is an [integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain) that can be endowed with a [[#Definition|Euclidean function]] which allows a suitable generalization of [Euclidean division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_division) of [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)s.

Euclidean plane isometry is an [isometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry) of the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane), or more informally, a way of transforming the plane that preserves geometrical properties such as length.
Euclidean space is the fundamental space of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry), intended to represent [physical space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_space).

Euler calculus is a methodology from applied [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) and [integral geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_geometry) that integrates [constructible function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructible_function)s and more recently [definable function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definable_function)s 219.
Euler system is a collection of compatible elements of [Galois cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_cohomology) groups indexed by [fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension).
Euler's four-square identity says that the product of two numbers, each of which is a sum of four [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_(algebra))s, is itself a sum of four squares.

Eulerian poset is a [graded poset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_poset) in which every nontrivial [[Partially ordered set#Intervals|interval]] has the same number of elements of even rank as of odd rank.

exact C*-algebra is a [C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebra) that preserves [exact sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exact_sequence)s under the [minimum tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_tensor_product).
exact category is a [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) equipped with [short exact sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_exact_sequence)s.
exact functor is a [functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functor) that preserves [short exact sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_exact_sequence)s.

quasi-excellent ring is a [Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) that behaves well with respect to the operation of [completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_of_a_ring), and is called an excellent ring if it is also [universally catenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_catenary).

exceptional field theory is a reformulation or an extension of [eleven-dimensional supergravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleven-dimensional_supergravity) in which [exceptional Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exceptional_Lie_algebra) symmetries are manifest.

exceptional isomorphisms of classical groups (also: accidental isomorphism or sporadic isogenies) are unexpected coincidences between different families of [symmetry group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_group)s in small dimensions.

exceptional Lie algebra is a complex [simple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Lie_algebra) whose [Dynkin diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynkin_diagram) is of exceptional (nonclassical) type.

genus of a multiplicative sequence is a [ring homomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_homomorphism) from the [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) of smooth [compact manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_manifold)s up to the equivalence of bounding a smooth manifold with boundary (i.e., up to suitable [cobordism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobordism)) to another ring, usually the [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number)s, having the property that they are constructed from a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence) of polynomials in [characteristic classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_classes) that arise as coefficients in formal [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series) with good multiplicative properties.

Geoffrey Horrocks (1932/33 [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester) – 12 September 2012) was a British mathematician working on [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s, who introduced the [Horrocks construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horrocks_construction) used in the [ADHM construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADHM_construction), and the [Horrocks–Mumford bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horrocks–Mumford_bundle) and [monads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monad_(homological_algebra)).

Geometriae Dedicata is a [mathematical journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_journal), founded in 1972, concentrating on [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) and its relationship to [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology), [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory) and the theory of [dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system)s.

geometric algebra (also known as a [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra)) is an [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) that can represent and manipulate geometrical objects such as [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_(mathematics_and_physics))s.

geometric class field theory is an extension of [class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory) to higher-dimensional geometrical objects: much the same way as class field theory describes the [abelianization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelianization) of the [Galois group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_group) of a [local](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field) or [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field), geometric class field theory describes the abelianized [fundamental group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group) of higher dimensional [schemes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) in terms of data related to [algebraic cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycle)s.

geometric genus is a basic [birational invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_invariant) of [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_varieties) and [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold)s.

geometric group action is a certain type of [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) of a [discrete group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_group) on a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space).

Geometric group theory is an area in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) devoted to the study of [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group)s via exploring the connections between [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra)ic properties of such [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) and [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) and [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) properties of spaces on which these groups can [act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) non-trivially (that is, when the groups in question are realized as geometric symmetries or continuous transformations of some spaces).

geometric invariant theory (or GIT) is a method for constructing quotients by [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics))s in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), used to construct [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space)s.

Grigorchuk group or the first Grigorchuk group is a [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group) constructed by [Rostislav Grigorchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rostislav_Grigorchuk) that provided the first example of a [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group) of intermediate (that is, faster than polynomial but slower than exponential) [growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growth_rate_(group_theory)).

Hochschild–Mostow group, introduced by , is the universal pro-affine [algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_group) generated by a group.

Hodge algebra or algebra with straightening law is a [commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra) that is a [free module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_module) over some [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) R, together with a given basis similar to the basis of [standard monomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_monomial)s of the [coordinate ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_ring) of a [Grassmannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassmannian).

Hodge–Arakelov theory of [elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve)s is an analogue of classical and [p-adic Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_Hodge_theory) for elliptic curves carried out in the framework of [Arakelov theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arakelov_theory).
Hodge–Tate module is an analogue of a [Hodge structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_structure) over [p-adic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_field)s.

homeomorphism group of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is the [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) consisting of all [homeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism)s from the space to itself with [function composition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_composition) as the group [operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation).

homeotopy group of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is a [homotopy group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_group) of the group of [self-homeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism)s of that space.

homogeneous function is a [function of several variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_variables) such that the following holds: If each of the function's arguments is multiplied by the same [scalar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_(mathematics)), then the function's value is multiplied by some power of this scalar; the power is called the degree of homogeneity, or simply the degree.

homogeneous polynomial, sometimes called [[wikt:quantic|quantic]] in older texts, is a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) whose nonzero terms all have the same [degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_a_polynomial).
homogeneous variety is an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) on which an [algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_group) acts transitively.

Homological algebra is the branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) that studies [homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_(mathematics)) in a general algebraic setting.

homological stability is any of a number of theorems asserting that the [group homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology) of a series of groups is related, via the +-construction, to the [algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory) of R.

homology manifold (or generalized manifold) is a [locally compact topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact_topological_space) X that looks locally like a [topological manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_manifold) from the point of view of [homology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_theory).

homomorphic secret sharing is a type of [secret sharing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_sharing) [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) in which the secret is encrypted via [homomorphic encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homomorphic_encryption).

homotopical algebra is a collection of concepts comprising the nonabelian aspects of [homological algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_algebra), and possibly the [abelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category) aspects as special cases.

Hopf algebra, named after [Heinz Hopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Hopf), is a structure that is simultaneously a ([unital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unital_algebra) associative) [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) and a (counital coassociative) [coalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalgebra), with these structures' compatibility making it a [bialgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bialgebra), and that moreover is equipped with an [antihomomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antihomomorphism) satisfying a certain property.

Malvenuto–Poirier–Reutenauer Hopf algebra of permutations or MPR Hopf algebra is a [Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_algebra) with a basis of all elements of all the finite symmetric groups S n} while preserving their order.
Hopf algebroid is a generalisation of weak Hopf algebras, certain skew Hopf algebras and commutative Hopf k-algebroids.

Hopfian group is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) G for which every [[Group homomorphism#Types of homomorphic maps|epimorphism]] :G → G is an [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism).
hopfian object is an object A such that any [epimorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epimorphism) of A onto A is necessarily an [automorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism).

Hopf–Whitney theorem is a result relating the [homotopy classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_classes) between a [CW complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CW_complex) and a multiply connected space with [singular cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_cohomology) classes of the former with coefficients in the first nontrivial [homotopy group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_group) of the latter.
Horikawa surface is one of the [surfaces of general type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surfaces_of_general_type) introduced by [Eiji Horikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiji_Horikawa).
Horrocks bundles are certain indecomposable rank 3 [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s (locally free sheaves) on 5-dimensional projective space, found by .

horseshoe lemma, also called the simultaneous resolution theorem, is a statement relating [resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_resolution)s of two objects .

Horst Knörrer (born 31 July 1953, in [Bayreuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayreuth)) is a German mathematician who studies [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and [mathematical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_physics).

definition: House with two rooms or Bing's house is a particular [contractible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contractible), 2-dimensional [simplicial complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplicial_complex) that is not [collapsible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_(topology)).

Householder transformation (also known as a Householder reflection or elementary reflector) is a [linear transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_transformation) that describes a [reflection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflection_(mathematics)) about a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)) or [hyperplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperplane) containing the origin.

Howson property, also known as the finitely generated intersection property (FGIP), is the property of a group saying that the intersection of any two finitely generated subgroups of this group is again finitely generated.
Hudde's rules are two [properties of polynomial roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_polynomial_roots) described by [Johann Hudde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Hudde).

Humbert surface, studied by , is a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)) in the [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space) of principally polarized [abelian surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_surface)s consisting of the surfaces with a symmetric [endomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endomorphism) of some fixed [discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant).

Hundred Fowls Problem is a problem first discussed in the fifth century CE [Chinese mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_mathematics) text [Zhang Qiujian suanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Qiujian_Suanjing) (The Mathematical Classic of Zhang Qiujian), a book of mathematical problems written by Zhang Qiujian.

Hurewicz theorem is a basic result of [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology), connecting [homotopy theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_theory) with [homology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_theory) via a map known as the Hurewicz homomorphism.
Hurwitz determinants were introduced by , who used them to give a criterion for all roots of a polynomial to have negative real part.

Hurwitz problem (named after [Adolf Hurwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hurwitz)) is the problem of finding multiplicative relations between [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form)s which generalise those known to exist between sums of squares in certain numbers of variables.

Hurwitz quaternion order is a specific [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(ring_theory)) in a [quaternion algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion_algebra) over a suitable [number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_field).

Hurwitz spaces are [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space)s of ramified [covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space) of the [projective line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_line), and they are related to the [moduli of curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_curves).

Hurwitz's theorem is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) of [Adolf Hurwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hurwitz), published posthumously in 1923, solving the [Hurwitz problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_problem) for [finite-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_(vector_space)) [unital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unital_algebra) [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) [non-associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-associative_algebra)s endowed with a nondegenerate [positive-definite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definite_quadratic_form) [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form).

hyper-finite field is an [uncountable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncountable_set) [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) similar in many ways to [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field)s.

hyperbolic group, also known as a word hyperbolic group or Gromov hyperbolic group, is a finitely generated [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) equipped with a [word metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_metric) satisfying certain properties abstracted from classical [hyperbolic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry).

definition: hyperdeterminant is a generalization of the [determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant).

hyperelliptic surface, or bi-elliptic surface, is a minimal [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)) whose [Albanese morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albanese_morphism) is an [elliptic fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_fibration) without singular fibres.

hyperfunctions are generalizations of functions, as a 'jump' from one [holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function) to another at a boundary, and can be thought of informally as [distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(mathematics))s of infinite order.

hyperplane is a generalization of a [two-dimensional plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) in [three-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) to [mathematical spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_(mathematics)) of arbitrary [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension).
hyperreal numbers are the elements of one of several possible [field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension)s 370.
hyperspecial subgroup of a reductive group G is a certain type of compact subgroup of G.

Hyperstructures are [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure)s equipped with at least one [multi-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-valued) operation, called a hyperoperation.

hypersurface is a generalization of the concepts of [hyperplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperplane), [plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_curve), and [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)).

hypertoric variety or toric hyperkähler variety is a [quaternion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion)ic analog of a [toric variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toric_variety) constructed by applying the hyper-Kähler quotient construction of to a torus acting on a [quaternionic vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternionic_vector_space).
hypoalgebra is a generalization of a [subalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subalgebra) of a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) introduced by .

High Performance Preconditioners (hypre) is a library of [routines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Source_code) for [scalable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalability) ([parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_computing)) solution of linear systems.

adic topologies are a family of [topologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) on the underlying set of a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)), generalizing the [-adic topologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number) on the [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)s.

IA automorphism of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) is an [automorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism) that acts as identity on the [abelianization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelianization).

Iacopo Barsotti, or Jacopo Barsotti (Turin, 28 April 1921 – Padua, 27 October 1987) was an Italian mathematician who introduced [Barsotti–Tate group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barsotti–Tate_group)s.

icosian calculus is a non-commutative [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) discovered by the Irish mathematician [William Rowan Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rowan_Hamilton) in 1856.
ideal of a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) is a special [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset) of its elements.
ideal is a special subset of a [partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set) (poset).
