definition: norm of an ideal is a generalization of a [norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_norm) of an element in the [field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension).
ideal theory is the theory of [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory))s in [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring)s.
idealizer of a subsemigroup T of a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) S is the largest subsemigroup of S in which T is an [[Semigroup#Subsemigroups and ideals|ideal]].

idele group is a way of packaging the multiplicative arithmetic of a [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field) at all of its completions at once, so that it contains the information of [unique factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_factorization) as well as the data relating to [units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_unit_theorem).
idempotent element or simply idempotent of a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) is an element such that is an idempotent such that .
idempotent matrix is a [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) which, when multiplied by itself, yields itself.

idempotent measure on a [metric group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_group) is a [probability measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_measure) that equals its [convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution) with itself; in other words, an idempotent measure is an [idempotent element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotent_element) in the [topological semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_semigroup) of probability measures on the given metric group.
identity element or neutral element of a [binary operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation) is an element that leaves unchanged every element when the operation is applied.

Igusa curve is (roughly) a coarse [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space) of [elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve)s in characteristic p with a level p Igusa structure, where an Igusa structure on an elliptic curve E is roughly a point of order p of E E.
Ihara zeta function is a [zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_function) associated with a finite [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)).

ILNumerics is a mathematical [class library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_(computing)) for [Common Language Infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Language_Infrastructure) (CLI) developers and a [domain specific language (DSL)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain-specific_language) for the [implementation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implementation) of [numerical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_analysis) [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm)s on the [.NET platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.NET_Framework).

definition: imaginary curve is an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) which does not contain any [real point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_point)s.
imaginary line is a [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)) that only contains one [real point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_point).

imaginary unit, usually denoted by , is a [mathematical constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_constant) that is a solution to the [quadratic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_equation) , which is not solved by any [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number).

incidence algebra is an [associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra), defined for every [locally finite partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_finite_partially_ordered_set) and [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) with unity.

incidence matrix is a [logical matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_matrix) that shows the relationship between two classes of objects, usually called an [incidence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_(geometry)).

incomplete Cholesky factorization of a symmetric [positive definite matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_definite_matrix) is a [sparse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_matrix) approximation of the [Cholesky factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholesky_factorization).

ind-scheme is a set-valued [functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functor) that can be written (represented) as a [direct limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_limit) (i.e., inductive limit) of [closed embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_immersion) of [schemes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)).

index calculus algorithm is a [probabilistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic) [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) for computing [discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_logarithm)s.

index of a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) H in a group G is the number of left [cosets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coset) of H in G, or equivalently, the number of right cosets of H in G.

induced character is the [character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_(mathematics)) of the [representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_representation) V of a [finite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_group) G [induced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_representation) from a representation W of a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) H ≤ G.
induced homomorphism is a [homomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homomorphism) derived in a canonical way from another map.

induced representation is a [representation of a group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_representation), , which is constructed using a known representation of a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) .

infinite expression is an [expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expression_(mathematics)) in which some [operators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_(mathematics)) take an infinite number of [arguments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_of_a_function), or in which the nesting of the operators continues to an infinite depth.

infinite group is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) whose [underlying set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forgetful_functor) contains [infinitely many](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_set) [element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Element_(mathematics))s.
infinite-dimensional sphere is the [inductive limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inductive_limit) of all [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)s.
infinitesimal cohomology is a [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory) for [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) introduced by .

inflation-restriction exact sequence is an [exact sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exact_sequence) occurring in [group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology) and is a special case of the [five-term exact sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five-term_exact_sequence) arising from the study of [spectral sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_sequences).

infraparticle is an electrically charged particle together with its surrounding cloud of [soft photon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_photon)s—of which there are an infinite number, by virtue of the [infrared divergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_divergence) of [quantum electrodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_electrodynamics).

infrared divergence (also IR divergence or infrared catastrophe) is a situation in which an [integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral), for example a [Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram), diverges because of contributions of objects with very small [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy) approaching zero, or equivalently, because of physical phenomena at very long distances.

infrared fixed point is a set of coupling constants, or other parameters, that evolve from arbitrary initial values at very high energies (short distance) to fixed, stable values, usually predictable, at low energies (large distance).
infrastructure is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics))-like structure appearing in [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field)s.
initial and final state radiation refers to certain kinds of radiative emissions that are not due to [particle annihilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_annihilation).

injective module is a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) Q that shares certain desirable properties with the Z-module Q of all [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number)s.

injective sheaves of [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group)s are used to construct the [resolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_(algebra)) needed to define [sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_cohomology) (and other [derived functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derived_functor)s, such as sheaf [Ext](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ext_functor)).

inner automorphism is an [automorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism) of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)), [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)), or [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) given by the [[Conjugacy class#Conjugacy as group action|conjugation action]] of a fixed element, called the conjugating element.
inner form of an [algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_group) , and they are inner forms of each other.

integer is the [number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number) zero ([0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/0)), a positive [natural number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_number) (1, 2, 3, ...), or the negation of a positive natural number ([−1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/−1), −2, −3, ...).

definition: integral over a [subring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subring) A of B if b is a [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_polynomial) of some [monic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monic_polynomial) over A.

integrally closed domain A is an [integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain) whose [integral closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_element) in its [field of fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_of_fractions) is A itself.

Inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUT or IUTT) is the name given by mathematician [Shinichi Mochizuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinichi_Mochizuki) to a theory he developed in the 2000s, following his earlier work in [arithmetic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_geometry).

interior algebra is a certain type of [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) that encodes the idea of the topological [interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_(topology)) of a set.

Ivan Aleksandrovich Panin (Иван Александрович Панин, born 2 July 1959 in [Apatity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apatity), Russia) is a Russian mathematician, specializing in [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra), [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), and [algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory).

Iwahori subgroup is a subgroup of a [reductive algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_algebraic_group) over a nonarchimedean [local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field) that is analogous to a [Borel subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_subgroup) of an algebraic group.

Iwahori–Hecke algebra, or Hecke algebra, named for [Erich Hecke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Hecke) and [Nagayoshi Iwahori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagayoshi_Iwahori), is a deformation of the [group algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_ring) of a [Coxeter group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coxeter_group).
Iwasawa theory is the study of objects of arithmetic interest over infinite [towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_fields) of [number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_field)s.
J-0 ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) .
j-multiplicity is a generalization of a [Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert–Samuel_multiplicity).

J-structure is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(algebra)) related to a [Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra).

Jacobi bound problem concerns the veracity of Jacobi's inequality which is an [inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inequality_(mathematics)) on the [absolute dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_dimension) of a [differential algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebraic_variety) in terms of its defining equations.

Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm is an [iterative method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterative_method) for the calculation of the [eigenvalue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalue)s and [eigenvector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvector)s of a [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) [symmetric matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_matrix) (a process known as [[Matrix diagonalization#Diagonalization|diagonalization]]).

Jacobi identity is a property of a [binary operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation) that describes how the order of evaluation, the placement of parentheses in a multiple product, affects the result of the operation.

Jacobian conjecture is a famous unsolved problem concerning [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s in several [variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_(mathematics)).

Jacobian ideal or gradient ideal is the [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) generated by the [Jacobian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant) of a function or [function germ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_(mathematics)).

Jacobian variety J(C) of a non-singular [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) C of [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus_(mathematics)) g is the [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space) of degree 0 [line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_bundle)s.
Jacobson density theorem is a theorem concerning [simple module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_module)s over a ring .

Hilbert ring or a Jacobson ring is a ring such that every [prime ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_ideal) is an intersection of [primitive ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_ideal)s.

Jacobson's conjecture is an [open problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_problem) in [ring theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_theory) concerning the [intersection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_(set_theory)) of powers of the [Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical) of a [Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)).

Jacobson–Bourbaki theorem is a theorem used to extend [Galois theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_theory) to [field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension)s that need not be separable.

Jaffard ring is a type of [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)), more general than a [Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring), for which [Krull dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_dimension) behaves as expected in polynomial extensions.

James reduced product or James construction J(X) of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) X with given basepoint e is the [quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_space_(topology)) of the [disjoint union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint_union) of all powers X, X ).

Janet basis is a [normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_form) for systems of linear homogeneous [partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation)s (PDEs) that removes the inherent arbitrariness of any such system.

Jantzen filtration is a [filtration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filtration_(mathematics)) of a [Verma module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verma_module) of a [semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra), or a [Weyl module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_module) of a [reductive algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_algebraic_group) of positive characteristic.

Jean-Pierre Serre (; born 15 September 1926) is a French [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) who has made contributions to [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology), [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and [algebraic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_theory).

John Brittain Little (born 1956) is a retired American mathematician, the author of several books in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and the [history of mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics).

John Greenlees Semple (10 June 1904 in [Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast), Ireland – 23 October 1985 in [London, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London,_England)) was a British mathematician working in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).
joint spectral radius is a generalization of the classical notion of [spectral radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_radius) of a matrix, to sets of matrices.
Jonathan Wahl is a mathematician based at the [University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_at_Chapel_Hill).

Jordan–Pólya numbers are the numbers that can be obtained by multiplying together one or more [factorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorial)s, not required to be distinct from each other.
Jordan–Schur theorem also known as Jordan's theorem on finite linear groups is a theorem in its original form due to [Camille Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Jordan).

Kirchhoff's theorem or Kirchhoff's matrix tree theorem is a theorem about the number of [spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanning_tree)s in a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)).

KK-theory is a common generalization both of [K-homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-homology) and [K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory) as an additive [[functor#Bifunctors|bivariant functor]] on [separable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separable_space) [C*-algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebras).

Klaus Hulek (born 19 August 1952 in [Bad Hindelang)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Hindelang) is a German mathematician, known for his work in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and in particular on [moduli spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space).

definition: Kleene algebra ( ; named after [Stephen Cole Kleene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Cole_Kleene)) is a [semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring) that generalizes the theory of [regular expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression)s: it consists of a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) supporting union (addition), concatenation (multiplication), and [Kleene star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleene_star) operations subject to certain algebraic laws.

Klein configuration, studied by , is a [geometric configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_configuration) related to [Kummer surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kummer_surface)s that consists of 60 points and 60 planes, with each point lying on 15 planes and each plane passing through 15 points.
Kleinian integer is a [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) of the form [[Category:Quadratic irrational numbers]] [[Category:Ring theory]] p6y0e0nj7udy25k7uvz78qcxm2ciyde

Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations, or KZ equations, are linear differential equations satisfied by the [correlation functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_function_(quantum_field_theory)) (on the [Riemann sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_sphere)) of [two-dimensional conformal field theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_conformal_field_theory) associated with an [affine Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_Lie_algebra) at a fixed level.
Koecher–Vinberg theorem is a reconstruction theorem for real [Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra)s.

Kolchin's problems are a set of [unsolved problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_problem) in [differential algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra), outlined by [Ellis Kolchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_Kolchin) at the [International Congress of Mathematicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Congress_of_Mathematicians) in 1966 (Moscow) == Kolchin Catenary Conjecture == The Kolchin Catenary Conjecture is a fundamental open problem in [differential algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra) related to [dimension theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_theory).

Konishi anomaly is the violation of the conservation of the [Noether current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether_current) associated with certain transformations in theories with N=1 [supersymmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry).

Koszul complex was first introduced to define a [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory) for [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra)s, by [Jean-Louis Koszul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Louis_Koszul) (see [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology)).

Koszul duality, named after the French mathematician [Jean-Louis Koszul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Louis_Koszul), is any of various kinds of [dualities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_(mathematics)) found in representation theory of [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra)s, abstract algebras ([semisimple algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_algebra)) mentioned above.

Koszul–Tate resolution or Koszul–Tate complex of the [quotient ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_ring) R/M is a [projective resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_resolution) of it as an R-module which also has a structure of a [dg-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dg-algebra) over R, where R is a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) and M ⊂ R is an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)).

Krasner's lemma is a basic result relating the [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) of a [complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_field) [non-archimedean field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-archimedean_field) to its [algebraic extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_extension)s.

Kronecker substitution is a technique named after [Leopold Kronecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Kronecker) for determining the coefficients of an unknown [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) by evaluating it at a single value.

Krull dimension of a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) R, named after [Wolfgang Krull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Krull), is the [supremum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supremum) of the lengths of all [chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_(order_theory))s of [prime ideals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_ideals).
Krull ring, or Krull domain, is a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) with a well behaved theory of prime factorization.
Krull's separation lemma is a [lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemma_(mathematics)) in [ring theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_theory).

Krylov subspace generated by an n-by-n [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) A and a vector b of dimension n is the [linear subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_subspace) [spanned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_span) by the [images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_(matrix)) of b under the first r powers of A (starting from , giving rise to [matrix-free methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix-free_methods).

Kuen surface is a [mathematical surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_surface) of constant negative unit [Gaussian curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_curvature), making it an example of a [pseudospherical surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudospherical_surface).

Kuga fiber variety, introduced by , is a [fiber space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle) whose fibers are [abelian varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety) and whose base space is an [arithmetic quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_variety) of a [Hermitian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_symmetric_space).

Kummer configuration, named for [Ernst Kummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Kummer), is a [geometric configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_configuration) of 16 points and 16 planes such that each point lies on 6 of the planes and each plane contains 6 of the points.

Kummer quartic surface, first studied by , is an [irreducible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreducible_space) [nodal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nodal_surface) of degree 4 in [[Projective_space#Definition_of_projective_space| configuration.

Kurosh subgroup theorem describes the algebraic structure of [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup)s of [free product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_product)s of [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)).

Kähler manifold is a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) with three mutually compatible structures: a [complex structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold), a [Riemannian structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold), and a [symplectic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold).
Köthe conjecture is a problem in [ring theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_theory), [open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_problem) .

Landau's function g(n), named after [Edmund Landau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Landau), is defined for every [natural number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_number) n to be the largest [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(group_theory)) of an element of the [symmetric group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_group) S 240.

Latimer–MacDuffee theorem is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) in [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra), a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics).

lattice is an abstract structure studied in the [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical) subdisciplines of [order theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_theory) and [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra).
lattice field theory is the study of [lattice models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_model_(physics)) of [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory).

lattice basis reduction is to find a [basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_(linear_algebra)) with short, nearly [orthogonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal) vectors when given an integer [lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(group)) basis as input.

law of total cumulance is a generalization to [cumulant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulant)s of the [law of total probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_total_probability), the [law of total expectation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_total_expectation), and the [law of total variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_total_variance).

The law of total variance is a fundamental result in [probability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_theory) that expresses the variance of a random variable in terms of its conditional variances and conditional means given another random variable .
Lawrence Man Hou Ein (born 18 November 1955) is a mathematician who works in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

Lazard's universal ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) introduced by [Michel Lazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Lazard) in over which the universal commutative one-dimensional [formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_group_law) is defined.

Le Potier's vanishing theorem is an extension of the [Kodaira vanishing theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_vanishing_theorem), on [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s.

Least-squares spectral analysis (LSSA) is a class of methods for estimating a [[Spectral density estimation#Overview|frequency spectrum]] by fitting [sinusoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_wave)s to data using a [least-squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least-squares) fit.
Leavitt path algebra is an [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) constructed from a directed graph.

Lefschetz theorem on (1,1)-classes, named after [Solomon Lefschetz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Lefschetz), is a classical statement relating holomorphic [line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_bundle)s on a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_manifold) to classes in its integral [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology).

(right) Leibniz algebra, named after [Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottfried_Wilhelm_Leibniz), sometimes called a Loday algebra, after [Jean-Louis Loday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Louis_Loday), is a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) L over a commutative ring R with a bilinear product [ _ , _ ] satisfying the Leibniz identity : ==Notes== ==References== * * * * * * * [[Category:Lie algebras]] [[Category:Non-associative algebras
Leibniz operator is a tool used to classify [deductive system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deductive_system)s, which have a precise technical definition and capture a large number of logics.
length function is a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) that assigns a number to each element of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)).

level structure on a [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_(mathematics)) X is an extra structure attached to X that shrinks or eliminates the [automorphism group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism_group) of X, by demanding automorphisms to preserve the level structure; attaching a level structure is often phrased as rigidifying the geometry of X.

Levitzky's theorem, named after [Jacob Levitzki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Levitzki), states that in a right [Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring), every nil one-sided [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) is necessarily [nilpotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilpotent_ideal).
Lie algebra (pronounced ) is a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) == Generalization == Several generalizations of a Lie algebra have been proposed, many from physics.
Lie algebra cohomology is a [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology) theory for [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra)s.

Lie algebra representation or representation of a Lie algebra is a way of writing a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) as a set of [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) (or [endomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endomorphism)s of a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)) in such a way that the Lie bracket is given by the [commutator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutator).
Lie-algebra-valued form is a [differential form with values in a Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector-valued_differential_form).

Lie bialgebra is the Lie-theoretic case of a [bialgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bialgebra): it is a set with a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) and a [Lie coalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_coalgebra) structure which are compatible.
Lie coalgebra is the dual structure to a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra).
Lie conformal algebra is in some sense a generalization of a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) in that it too is a .

Lie n-algebra is a [generalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalization_of_a_Lie_algebra) of a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra), a vector space with a bracket, to higher order operations.
Lie operad is an [operad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operad_theory) [whose algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operad_algebra) are [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra)s.
Lie superalgebra is a generalisation of a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) to include a pg=PA1|series=Courant Lecture Notes in Mathematics|volume=11}} === Historical === *.
Lie-* algebra is a [D-module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-module) with a Lie* bracket.

Lie-admissible algebra, introduced by , is a (possibly [non-associative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-associative_algebra)) [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) that becomes a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) under the bracket [a, Lie algebras, and [Okubo algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okubo_algebra)s.

Lie–Kolchin theorem is a theorem in the [representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory) of [linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group)s; [Lie's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie's_theorem) is the analog for [linear Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_Lie_algebra)s.

Lie–Palais theorem is a partial converse to the fact that any [smooth action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group_action) of a [Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group) induces an infinitesimal action of its [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra).
Light's associativity test is a procedure invented by F.

lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) is the generic name given to the lightest of the additional hypothetical particles found in [supersymmetric models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_Supersymmetric_Standard_Model).
like terms are [summand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summand)s in a [sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summation) that differ only by a numerical factor.

limit groups are the [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group)s that admit a [presentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presentation_of_a_group) which is a limit of [free group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_group) presentations in the discrete [Chabauty topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chabauty_topology).

Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra (or Lindenbaum algebra) of a [[model theory#Definition|logical theory]] T consists of the [equivalence class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_class)es of [sentence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentence_(mathematical_logic))s of the theory (i.e., the [quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_class)) under the [equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation) ~ defined such that p ~ q exactly when p and q are provably equivalent in T.
line complex is a set of lines that can be specified by a list of [homogeneous polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_polynomial) equations.

line segment is a part of a [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(mathematics)) that is bounded by two distinct endpoints (its [extreme point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_point)s), and contains every [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) on the line that is between its endpoints.

[linear equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_equation)s and [systems of linear equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_of_linear_equations) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) are widely studied.

matrix group is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) G consisting of [invertible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invertible_matrix) [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) over a specified [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K, with the operation of [matrix multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_multiplication).

linear map (or linear mapping) is a particular kind of [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) between [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s, which respects the basic operations of [vector addition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_addition) and [scalar multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_multiplication).

linear relation, or simply relation, between elements of a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) or a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) is a [linear equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_equation) that has these elements as a solution.

linked field is a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(algebra)) for which the [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form)s attached to [quaternion algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion_algebra)s have a common property.

Liouville field theory (or simply Liouville theory) is a [two-dimensional conformal field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_conformal_field_theory) whose classical [equation of motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation_of_motion) is a generalization of [Liouville's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville's_equation).
Liouville space, also known as line space, is the space of operators on [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space).

algebraic construction is a method by which an [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra)ic entity is defined or derived from another.

operad is a structure that consists of abstract [operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_(mathematics)), each one having a fixed finite number of inputs (arguments) and one output, as well as a specification of how to compose these operations.

operand is the [object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_object) of a [mathematical operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_(mathematics)), i.e., it is the object or quantity that is operated on.

operator is generally a [mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Map_(mathematics)) or [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) that acts on elements of a [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_(mathematics)) to produce elements of another space (possibly and sometimes required to be the same space).

operator algebra is an [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) of [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function_(topology)) [linear operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_operator)s on a [topological vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_vector_space), with the multiplication given by the [composition of mappings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_composition).

operator K-theory is a [noncommutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noncommutative_topology) analogue of [topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory) for [Banach algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebras) with most applications used for [C*-algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebras).
operator product expansion (OPE) is used as an axiom to define the product of fields as a sum over the same fields.
opposite of a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) is another ring with the same elements and addition operation, but with the multiplication performed in the reverse order.

Optimization Programming Language (OPL) is an [algebraic modeling language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_modeling_language) for [mathematical optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_optimization) models, which makes the coding easier and shorter than with a general-purpose programming language.
OR gate is a digital [logic gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_gate) that implements [logical disjunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction).

[orbifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbifold) notation (or orbifold signature) is a system, invented by the mathematician [William Thurston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thurston) and promoted by [John Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Horton_Conway), for representing types of [symmetry groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_groups) in two-dimensional spaces of constant curvature.
order of a [finite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_group) is the number of its elements.

definition: order operator or an order field is a [quantum field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field) version of Landau's [order parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_parameter) whose expectation value characterizes [phase transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition)s.

ordered exponential, also called the path-ordered exponential, is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) operation defined in [non-commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-commutative) [algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field), equivalent to the [exponential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function) of the [integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral) in the [commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative) algebras.

ordered exponential field is an [ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field) together with a function which generalises the idea of exponential functions on the ordered field of real numbers.

ordered field is a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) together with a [total order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_order)ing of its elements that is compatible with the field operations.

ordered ring is a (usually [commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring)) [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) R with a [total order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_order) ≤ such that for all a, b, and c in R: as either b or −b is positive, a must be nonnegative.

ordered semigroup is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) (S,•) together with a [partial order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_order) ≤ that is compatible with the semigroup operation, meaning that x ≤ y implies z•x ≤ z•y and x•z ≤ y•z for all x, y, z in S.

ordinary singularity of an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) is a [singular point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_point_of_a_curve) of [multiplicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicity_(mathematics)) r where the r tangents at the point are distinct .

Ore algebra is a special kind of iterated [Ore extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore_extension) that can be used to represent linear functional operators, including linear differential and/or recurrence operators.

Ore condition is a condition introduced by [Øystein Ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Øystein_Ore), in connection with the question of extending beyond [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring)s the construction of a [field of fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_of_fractions), or more generally [localization of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Localization_of_a_ring).

Ore extension, named after [Øystein Ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Øystein_Ore), is a special type of a [ring extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_extension) whose properties are relatively well understood.

Pareigis Hopf algebra is the [Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_algebra) over a field k whose left [comodules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comodule) are essentially the same as complexes over k, in the sense that the corresponding [monoidal categories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoidal_category) are isomorphic.

definition: parity transformation (also called parity inversion) is the flip in the sign of one [spatial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) [coordinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate).

parity function is a [Boolean function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_function) whose value is one [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) the input vector has an odd number of ones.

Parry–Sullivan invariant (or Parry–Sullivan number) is a numerical quantity of interest in the study of [incidence matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_matrix) in [graph theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_theory), and of certain one-dimensional [dynamical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_systems).
Parshin chain is a higher-dimensional analogue of a [place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_(mathematics)) of an [algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field).
partial algebra is a generalization of [universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra) to [[Binary operation#Terminology|partial operation]]s.

partial fraction decomposition or partial fraction expansion of a [rational fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_fraction) (that is, a [fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraction_(mathematics)) such that the numerator and the denominator are both [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s) is an operation that consists of expressing the fraction as a sum of a polynomial (possibly zero) and one or several fractions with a simpler denominator.

partial group algebra is an [associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) related to the [partial representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_representation)s of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)).

partial [groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma_(algebra)) (also called halfgroupoid, pargoid, or partial magma) is a set endowed with a [[Binary operation#Terminology|partial binary operation]].

partial isometry is a [linear map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map) between [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space)s such that it is an [isometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry) on the [orthogonal complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal_complement) of its [kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_(algebra)).

partition functions are [generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function)als for [correlation functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_function_(quantum_field_theory)), making them key objects of study in the [path integral formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Path_integral_formulation).

Pascal's rule (or Pascal's formula) is a [combinatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics) [identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_(mathematics)) about [binomial coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient)s.

Pasquale del Pezzo, Duke of [Caianello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caianello) and Marquis of Campodisola (2 May 1859 – 20 June 1936), was an Italian [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician).

path integral formulation is a description in [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics) that generalizes the [stationary action principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_action_principle) of [classical mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_mechanics).
path-ordering is the procedure (or a [meta-operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-operator) ensures that this ordering will be preserved.

Pauli–Lubanski pseudovector is an [operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_(physics)) defined from the momentum and [angular momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_momentum), used in the [quantum-relativistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_quantum_mechanics) description of angular momentum.

Pauli–Villars regularization (P–V) is a procedure that isolates divergent terms from finite parts in loop calculations in [field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_theory_(physics)) in order to [renormalize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization) the theory.

pencil is a family of geometric objects with a common property, for example the set of [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry))s that pass through a given point in a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)), or the set of [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s that pass through two given points in a plane.

Penrose graphical notation or tensor diagram notation is a (usually handwritten) visual depiction of [multilinear function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multilinear_function)s or [tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor)s proposed by [Roger Penrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Penrose) in 1971.

perfect core (or perfect radical) of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) is its largest [perfect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_group) [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup).
perfect ideal is a proper [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) is a homogeneous ideal in a polynomial ring, but may differ otherwise.

persistence module is a [mathematical structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_structure) in [persistent homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persistent_homology) and [topological data analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_data_analysis) that formally captures the persistence of [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) features of an object across a range of scale parameters.

persistent Betti number is a multiscale analog of a [Betti number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betti_number) that tracks the number of [topological features](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_(mathematics)) that persist over multiple scale parameters in a [filtration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filtration_(mathematics)).

persistent homology group is a multiscale analog of a [homology group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_(mathematics)) that captures information about the evolution of [topological features](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) across a [filtration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filtration_(mathematics)) of spaces.

perverse sheaves refers to the objects of certain [abelian categories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category) associated to [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s, which may be a real or complex [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold), or more general [topologically stratified space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topologically_stratified_space)s, possibly singular.

Peter–Weyl theorem is a basic result in the theory of [harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis), applying to [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group)s that are [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group), but are not necessarily [abelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group).

photomagneton is a theoretical treatment of the [unitary group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_group) in [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) and [quantum chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_chemistry) that effectively describes the experimentally observed [inverse Faraday effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Faraday_effect).

Picard modular group, studied by , is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) of the form SU(J,L), where L is a 3-dimensional [lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(group)) over the [ring of integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_integers) of an [imaginary quadratic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_quadratic_field) and J is a [hermitian form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_form) on L of signature and the quotient is called a [Picard modular surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard_modular_surface).

Picard modular surface, studied by , is a [complex surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_surface) constructed as a quotient of the unit ball in C by a [Picard modular group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard_modular_group).

Picard–Vessiot theory is the study of the [differential field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_field) extension generated by the solutions of a [linear differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_differential_equation), using the [differential Galois group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_Galois_group) of the field extension.

picture is a [bijection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijection) between [[Young tableau#Skew tableaux|skew diagrams]] satisfying certain properties, introduced by in a generalization of the [Robinson–Schensted correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson–Schensted_correspondence) and the [Littlewood–Richardson rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood–Richardson_rule).

piecewise algebraic space is a generalization of a [semialgebraic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semialgebraic_set), introduced by [Maxim Kontsevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim_Kontsevich) and [Yan Soibelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan_Soibelman).

definition: pinch point or cuspidal point is a type of [singular point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_point_of_an_algebraic_variety) on an [algebraic surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_surface).

definition: ping-pong lemma, or table-tennis lemma, is any of several mathematical statements that ensure that several elements in a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) [acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action) on a set freely [generates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_set_of_a_group) a [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_group) [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) of that group.

Pisier–Ringrose inequality is an inequality in the theory of C*-algebras which was proved by [Gilles Pisier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilles_Pisier) in 1978 affirming a conjecture of [John Ringrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ringrose).

Pisot–Vijayaraghavan number, also called simply a Pisot number or a PV number, is a [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) [algebraic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_integer) greater than 1, all of whose [Galois conjugate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_conjugate)s are less than 1 in [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value).

planar 3-satisfiability problem (abbreviated PLANAR 3SAT or PL3SAT) is an extension of the classical [[Boolean satisfiability problem#3-satisfiability|Boolean 3-satisfiability problem]] to a [planar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planar_graph) [incidence graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_graph).
plane of rotation is an abstract object used to describe or visualize [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation_(mathematics))s in space.

Plane-based geometric algebra is an application of [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra) to modelling planes, lines, points, and [rigid transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_transformation)s.

definition: plane-wave solutions to the Dirac equation, are standard [basis solutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_(linear_algebra)) to the [Dirac equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_equation) describing the propagation of [Dirac spinor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_spinor)s.

plus construction is a method for simplifying the [fundamental group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group) of a space without changing its [homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_(mathematics)) and [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology) [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics))s.

Plücker coordinates, introduced by [Julius Plücker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Plücker) in the 19th century, are a way to assign six [homogeneous coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_coordinates) to each [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(mathematics)) in [projective 3-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space), .

Plücker formula, named after [Julius Plücker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Plücker), is one of a family of formulae, of a type first developed by Plücker in the 1830s, that relate certain numeric invariants of [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve)s to corresponding invariants of their [dual curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_curve)s.
Pohlke's theorem is the fundamental theorem of [axonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axonometry).

Pohlmeyer charge, named for [[:de:Klaus Pohlmeyer|Klaus Pohlmeyer]], is a conserved [charge invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_invariance) under the [Virasoro algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virasoro_algebra) or its generalization.

Poincaré complex (named after the mathematician [Henri Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincaré)) is an abstraction of the [singular chain complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_chain_complex) of a [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_manifold), [orientable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientable_manifold) [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold).

Poincaré duality theorem, named after [Henri Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincaré), is a basic result on the structure of the [homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_(mathematics)) and [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology) [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics))s of [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s.

Poincaré gauge theory (PGT) is a [classical field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_field_theory) that describes [gravitational interactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity) as a [gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory) based on enforcing the [[Symmetry (physics)#Local and global|local]] [Poincaré group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_group)—the group consisting of [translations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_(geometry)) and [Lorentz rotations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_group).

Poincaré space is an n-dimensional [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) with a distinguished element μ of its nth [homology group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_group) such that taking the [cap product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_product) with an element of the kth [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology) group yields an isomorphism to the (n for instance, the Poincaré dodecahedral space in 3 dimensions.

Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem (or PBW theorem) is a result giving an explicit description of the [universal enveloping algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_enveloping_algebra) of a Lie algebra.

[point group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_group) in three dimensions is an [isometry group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry_group) in three dimensions that leaves the origin fixed, or correspondingly, an isometry group of a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere).

point reflection (also called a point inversion or central inversion) is a [geometric transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_transformation) of [affine space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_space) in which every [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) is reflected across a designated inversion center, which remains [fixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_point_(mathematics)).

Poisson ring is a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) on which an [anticommutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticommutativity) and [distributive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributivity) [binary operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation) is the Poisson bracket defined by the symplectic form.

polar point group is a [point group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_group) in which there is more than one point that every [symmetry operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_operation) leaves unmoved.

polarization is the maximal [totally isotropic subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotropic_quadratic_form) of a certain skew-symmetric [bilinear form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilinear_form) on a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra).
pole mass of an elementary particle is the limiting value of the [rest mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rest_mass) of a particle as the energy scale of measurement increases.

Polyadic algebras (more recently called Halmos algebras) are [algebraic structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) introduced by [Paul Halmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Halmos), designed to study [first-order logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-order_logic).

Polyakov action is an [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_(physics)) of the [two-dimensional conformal field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_conformal_field_theory) describing the [worldsheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worldsheet) of a string in [string theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory).

Polyakov loop is the thermal analogue of the [Wilson loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_loop), acting as an [order parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_operator) for [confinement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_confinement) in pure [gauge theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory) at nonzero [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature)s.
polynomial differential forms on the standard [n-simplex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex) is the [differential graded algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_graded_algebra): ).

greatest common divisor (frequently abbreviated GCD or gcd) of two [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s is a polynomial, of the highest possible degree, which is a [factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorization) of both the two original polynomials.

polynomial long division is an [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) for dividing a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) by another polynomial of the same or lower [degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_a_polynomial), a generalized version of the familiar arithmetic technique called [long division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_division).
polynomial map or polynomial mapping are (scalar-valued) [polynomial function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_function)s on V.
polynomial transformation consists of computing the polynomial whose [roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_polynomial) are a given function of the roots of a polynomial.

Pontryagin cohomology operation is a [cohomology operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_operation) taking [cohomology classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_class) in H also being used).

power iteration (also known as the power method) is an [eigenvalue algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalue_algorithm): given a [diagonalizable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonalizable) [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) is a super-linear and deterministic method to compute the largest eigenpair.
power-bounded element is an element of a [topological ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_ring) whose powers are bounded.

Prakash Belkale (born May 1973, [Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangalore)) is an Indian-American mathematician, specializing in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and [representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory).

Pre-algebra is a common name for a [course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Course_(education)) taught in [middle school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_school) [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) in the United States, usually taught in the 6th, 7th, 8th, or 9th grade.

preconditioning is the application of a transformation, called the preconditioner, that conditions a given problem into a form that is more suitable for [numerical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_mathematics) solving methods.

predicate functor logic (PFL) is one of several ways to express [first-order logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-order_logic) (also known as [predicate logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predicate_logic)) by purely algebraic means, i.e., without [quantified variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantification_(logic))s.
predual of an object D is an object P whose [dual space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space) is D.

presentation complex is a 2-dimensional [cell complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_complex) associated to any [presentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presentation_of_a_group) of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) G.
presentation is one method of specifying a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)).

presheaf with transfers is, roughly, a [presheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presheaf_(category_theory)) that, like [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory), comes with pushforwards, “transfer” maps.

primary field, also called a primary operator, or simply a primary, is a local operator in a [conformal field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_field_theory) which is annihilated by the part of the [conformal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_algebra) consisting of the lowering generators.

left primitive ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) which has a [faithful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faithful_module) [simple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_module) left [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)).
primordial element is a particular kind of a [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_(mathematics_and_physics)) in a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space).

principal axis is a certain line in a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) associated with a [ellipsoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsoid) or [hyperboloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperboloid), generalizing the major and minor [axes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_symmetry) of an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse) or [hyperbola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbola).
principal ideal is an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) has [height](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Height_(ring_theory)) at most one.

principal ideal domain, or PID, is an [integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain) (that is, a non-zero [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) without nonzero [zero divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_divisor)s) in which every [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) is [principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal) (that is, is formed by the multiples of a single element).

principal right (left) ideal ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) R in which every right (left) [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) is of the form xR (Rx) for some element x of R.

principal subalgebra of a [complex simple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_simple_Lie_algebra) is a 3-dimensional simple subalgebra whose non-zero elements are [regular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_element_of_a_Lie_algebra).

principalization (also called capitulation) refers to the phenomenon where an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) (or more generally a [fractional ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_ideal)) of the [ring of integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_integers) of a number field, which is not [principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal) in that field, becomes principal after extension to the ring of integers of a larger [algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field).

principle of distributivity states that the algebraic [distributive law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_law) is [valid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Validity_(logic)), where both [logical conjunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction) and [logical disjunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction) are distributive over each other.
