Rarita–Schwinger equation is the [relativistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity) field equation for [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics))-3/2 [fermion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermion)s.

ratio distribution (also known as a quotient distribution) is a [probability distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution) constructed as the distribution of the [ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratio) of [random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variable)s having two other known distributions.

rational conformal field theory is a special type of [two-dimensional conformal field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_conformal_field_theory) with a finite number of conformal [primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_field).

rational function is any [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) that can be defined by a rational fraction, which is an [algebraic fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_fraction) such that both the [numerator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerator) and the [denominator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denominator) are [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s.
rational map or rational mapping is a kind of [partial function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_function) between [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_varieties).
related: Function field of an algebraic variety

definition: rational monoid is a [monoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoid), an algebraic structure, for which each element can be represented in a ==Properties== Kleene's theorem holds for rational monoids: that is, a subset is a recognisable set if and only if it is a rational set.

rational normal curve is a smooth, [rational curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_curve) of [degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_an_algebraic_variety) in [projective n-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) of degree is a rational normal curve.

rational number is a [number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number) that can be expressed as the [quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient) or [fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraction_(mathematics)) of two [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)s, a [numerator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerator) and a nonzero [denominator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denominator) .

rational if, viewed as a map from the group to the [general linear group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_linear_group), it is a [rational map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_map) of algebraic varieties.

rational series is a generalisation of the concept of [formal power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_power_series) over a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) to the case when the basic algebraic structure is no longer a ring but a [semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring), and the [indeterminate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indeterminate_(variable))s adjoined are not assumed to [commute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_property).

rational surface is a surface [birationally equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry) to the [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane), or in other words a [rational variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety) of dimension two.

rational variety is an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety), over a given [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K, which is [birationally equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birationally_equivalent) to a [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) of some dimension over K.

ray class field is an [abelian extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_extension) of a [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field) associated with a ray class group of [ideal classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_class_group) or [idele classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character).
Raynaud surface is a particular kind of [algebraic surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_surface) that was introduced in and named for .

read-once function is a special type of [Boolean function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_function) that can be described by a [Boolean expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_expression) in which each [variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_(mathematics)) appears only once.
real algebraic geometry is the sub-branch of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) studying real [algebraic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_set)s, i.e.

real closed ring (RCR) is a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) A that is a [subring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subring) of a [product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_ring) of [real closed field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field)s, which is closed under [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function) [semi-algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semialgebraic_set) functions defined over the [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)s.

real number is a [number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number) that can be used to [measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurement) a [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_variable) one-[dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)al [quantity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantity) such as a [length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length), [duration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time) or [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature).

real projective space, denoted {{tmath|\mathbb{RP}^n}} or {{tmath|\mathbb{P}_n(\R),}} is the [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) of [lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(mathematics)) passing through the origin 0 in the [real space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_coordinate_space) {{tmath|\R^{n+1}.}} It is a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space), [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold) of [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension) , and is a special case {{tmath|\mathbf{Gr}(1, \R^{n+1})}} of a [Grassmannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassmannian) space.

real radical of an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) I in a [polynomial ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_ring) with [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) [coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient)s is the largest ideal containing I with the same (real) vanishing locus.

real rank of a [C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebra) is a [noncommutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noncommutative_topology) analogue of [Lebesgue covering dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_covering_dimension).

real-root isolation of a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) consist of producing disjoint [interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(mathematics))s of the [real line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_line), which contain each one (and only one) real [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_function) of the polynomial, and, together, contain all the real roots of the polynomial.

reciprocity law is a generalization of the [law of quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_quadratic_reciprocity) to arbitrary monic irreducible polynomials imply the Artin reciprocity law.
REDUCE is a general-purpose [computer algebra system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_algebra_system) originally geared towards applications in physics.
categories: Computer algebra system software for Linux

definition: reduct of an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) is obtained by omitting some of the [operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_(mathematics)) and [relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relation_(mathematics)) of that structure.
reduction refers to the [rewriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rewriting) of an [expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expression_(mathematics)) into a simpler form.
reductive group is a type of [linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)).
reductive if its [adjoint representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_endomorphism) is [completely reducible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_representation), hence the name.

Reeh–Schlieder theorem is a result in relativistic [local quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_quantum_field_theory) published by [Helmut Reeh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Reeh) and [Siegfried Schlieder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegfried_Schlieder) in 1961.
Rees decomposition is a way of writing a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) in terms of polynomial subrings.

Reflected entropy is a quantity in [quantum information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_information) theory that measures [correlations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation) in a bipartite [quantum-mechanical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics) system described by a [mixed state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_state_(physics)).

reflection theorem or Spiegelungssatz ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language) for reflection theorem – see [Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiegel_(disambiguation)) and [Satz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satz_(disambiguation))) is one of a collection of theorems linking the sizes of different [ideal class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_class_group)s (or [ray class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_class_group)s), or the sizes of different [isotypic component](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotypic_component)s of a class group.

reflexive operator algebra A is an [operator algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_algebra) that has enough [invariant subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace)s to characterize it.
Regev's theorem, proved by , states that the [tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product) of two [PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra)s is a PI algebra.

regular chain is a particular kind of triangular set of [multivariate polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_polynomial)s over a field, where a triangular set is a finite sequence of polynomials such that each one contains at least one more indeterminate than the preceding one.

definition: regular element of a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) or [Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group) is an element whose centralizer has dimension as small as possible.

regular homotopy refers to a special kind of [homotopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy) between [immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_(mathematics))s of one [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) in another.

regular local ring is a [Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) [local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring) having the property that the minimal number of [generators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_set_of_a_module) of its [maximal ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximal_ideal) is equal to its [Krull dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_dimension).

regular scheme is a [locally Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_Noetherian_scheme) [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) whose [local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring)s are [regular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring) everywhere.
regular semi-algebraic system is a particular kind of triangular system of multivariate polynomials over a real closed field.
regular semigroup is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) S in which every element is regular, i.e., for each element a in S there exists an element x in S such that .
regular sequence is a sequence of elements of a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) which are as independent as possible, in a precise sense.

regularization is a method of modifying [observables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observables) which have [singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_(mathematics)) in order to make them finite by the introduction of a suitable parameter called the regulator.

definition: Regularized least squares (RLS) is a family of methods for solving the [least-squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_squares) problem while using [regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_(mathematics)) to further constrain the resulting solution.
Reinhardt Kiehl (31 May 1935 – 26 January 2026) was a German mathematician.

relation algebra is a [residuated Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residuated_Boolean_algebra) [expanded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduct) with an [involution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Involution_(mathematics)) called converse, a [unary operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unary_operation).

Renormalization is a collection of techniques in [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory), [statistical field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_field_theory), and the theory of [self-similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-similarity) geometric structures, that is used to treat [infinities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity) arising in calculated quantities by altering values of these quantities to compensate for effects of their self-interactions Poincaré Seminar 2002, Progress in Mathematical Physics 30, Birkhäuser (2003) .

renormalization group (RG) is a formal apparatus that allows systematic investigation of the changes of a [physical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_system) as viewed at different [scales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scale_(analytical_tool)).
representation on coordinate rings is a [representation of a group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_of_a_group) on coordinate rings of affine varieties.

representation of a [Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_algebra) is a [representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_representation) of its underlying [associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra).

Research in Number Theory is a [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [mathematics journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_journal) covering [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) and [arithmetic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_geometry).
Reshetikhin–Turaev invariants (RT-invariants) are a family of [quantum invariants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_invariants) of [framed link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framed_link)s.

residuated Boolean algebra is a [residuated lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residuated_lattice) whose lattice structure is that of a [Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_(structure)).

residuated lattice is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) that is simultaneously a [lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(order)) x ≤ y and a [monoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoid) x•y that admits operations x\z and z/y, loosely analogous to division or implication, when x•y is viewed as multiplication or [conjunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction), respectively.
residue field is a basic construction in [commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra).

residue-class-wise affine [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) are certain [permutation groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_groups) [acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) on , though only little work in this direction has been done so far.

resolution (or left resolution; dually a coresolution or right resolution Similarly [Godement resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godement_resolution)s are acyclic with respect to the global sections functor.

resolvent for a [permutation group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_group) G is a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) whose [coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient)s depend polynomially on the coefficients of a given polynomial p and has, roughly speaking, a [rational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number) [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_polynomial) [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) the [Galois group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_group) of p is included in G.
restricted isometry property (RIP) characterizes [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) which are nearly orthonormal, at least when operating on sparse vectors.

restricted Lie algebra (or p-Lie algebra) is a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) of [characteristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_(algebra)) p ==Jacobson's Galois correspondence== [[purely inseparable extension#Galois correspondence for purely inseparable extensions|Jacobson's Galois correspondence]] for purely inseparable field extensions is expressed in terms of restricted Lie algebras.

restricted root systems, sometimes called relative root systems, are the [root system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_system)s associated with a [symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_space).

resultant of two [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s is a [polynomial expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_expression) of their coefficients that is equal to zero [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) the polynomials have a common [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_function) (possibly in a [field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension)), or, equivalently, a common [factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorization) (possibly in a field extension as well).

resummation is a procedure to obtain a finite result from a [divergent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series) sum (series) of [functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)).
ribbon Hopf algebra is finite-dimensional and quasi-triangular, then it is ribbon if and only if its category of (say, left) modules is pivotal.
Ribet's theorem (earlier called the epsilon conjecture or ε-conjecture) is part of [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory).

Richard Evan Schwartz (born August 11, 1966) is an American [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) notable for his contributions to [geometric group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_group_theory) and to an area of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) known as [billiards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard).

Ridge regression (also known as Tikhonov regularization, named for [Andrey Tikhonov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrey_Nikolayevich_Tikhonov)) is a method of estimating the [coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient)s of multiple-[regression model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_model)s in scenarios where the variables are highly correlated.

Riemann–Hurwitz formula, named after [Bernhard Riemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_Riemann) and [Adolf Hurwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hurwitz), describes the relationship of the [Euler characteristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_characteristic)s of two [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology))s when one is a ramified covering of the other.

Riemann–Roch theorem for smooth manifolds is a version of results such as the [Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch_theorem) or [Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch_theorem) (GRR) without a hypothesis making the [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold)s involved carry a [complex structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold).

rigid analytic space is an analogue of a [complex analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analytic_space) over a [nonarchimedean field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonarchimedean_field).

ring is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) consisting of a set with two [binary operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation)s typically called addition and multiplication and denoted like [addition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addition) and [multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplication) of integers.

ring class field is the [abelian extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_extension) of an [algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field) K associated by [class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory) to the ring class group of some [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(ring_theory)) O of the [ring of integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_integers) of K.
ring homomorphism is a structure-preserving [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) between two [rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)).

ring of mixed characteristic is a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) is an example of a [complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_(ring_theory)) [discrete valuation ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_valuation_ring) of mixed characteristic.

ring of modular forms associated to a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) of the [special linear group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_linear_group) is the [graded ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_ring) generated by the [modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form)s of .

ring of symmetric functions is a specific limit of the [rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) of [symmetric polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_polynomial)s in n indeterminates, as n goes to infinity.

Ringel–Hall algebra is a generalization of the [Hall algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_algebra), studied by .

Rouché–Capelli theorem is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) in [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra) that determines the number of [solutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solution_set) of a [system of linear equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_linear_equations), given the [rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank_(linear_algebra))s of its [augmented matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augmented_matrix) and [coefficient matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient_matrix).

Russo–Dye theorem is a result in the field of [functional analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_analysis).

R-function, or Rvachev function, is a [real-valued function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-valued_function) whose sign does not change if none of the signs of its arguments change; that is, its sign is determined solely by the signs of its arguments.

S-equivalence is an [equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation) on the families of [semistable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_vector_bundle) [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s on an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve).

S-matrix or scattering matrix is a [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) that relates the initial state and the final state of a physical system undergoing a [scattering process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scattering).

S-procedure or S-lemma is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) result that gives conditions under which a particular quadratic inequality is a consequence of another quadratic inequality.

Satake diagrams are a generalization of [Dynkin diagrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynkin_diagram) that classify involutions of root systems that are relevant in several contexts.

SBI ring is a type of [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) R (with identity) such that every [idempotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotent_(ring_theory)) of R [modulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo_(jargon)) the [Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical) can be [lifted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lift_(mathematics)) to R.

scalar boson is a [boson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boson) whose [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics)) equals zero.
scale invariance is a feature of objects or laws that do not change if scales of length, energy, or other variables, are multiplied by a common factor, and thus represent a universality.

Schmidt decomposition (named after its originator [Erhard Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erhard_Schmidt)) refers to a particular way of expressing a [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_vector) in the [tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product) of two [inner product space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space)s.

Scholz's reciprocity law is a [reciprocity law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_law) for quadratic residue symbols of real [quadratic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_number_field)s discovered by and rediscovered by .
Schoof's algorithm is an efficient algorithm to count points on [elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve)s over [finite fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_fields).

Schoof–Elkies–Atkin algorithm (SEA) is an [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) used for finding the [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(group_theory)) of or calculating the number of points on an [elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve) over a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field).
Schottky group is a special sort of [Kleinian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleinian_group), first studied by .

Schottky problem, named after [Friedrich Schottky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Schottky), is a classical question of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), asking for a characterisation of [Jacobian varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_varieties) amongst [abelian varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_varieties).

Schreier coset graph is a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) associated with a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) G, a [generating set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_set_of_a_group) of G, and a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) of G.

Schreier domain, named after [Otto Schreier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Schreier), is an [integrally closed domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrally_closed_domain) where every nonzero element is primal; i.e., whenever x divides yz, x can be written as x = x this generalizes the fact that an atomic GCD domain is a UFD.

Schreier vector is a tool for reducing the time and space complexity required to calculate [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_(group_theory)) of a [permutation group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_group).

Schreier's lemma is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) used in the [Schreier–Sims algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schreier–Sims_algorithm) and also for finding a [presentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presentation_of_a_group) of a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup).

Schreier–Sims algorithm is an [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) in [computational group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_group_theory), named after the mathematicians [Otto Schreier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Schreier) and [Charles Sims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Sims_(mathematician)).
M is a [von Neumann algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_algebra) and E, F are projections in M.
Schrödinger functional is, in its most basic form, the [time translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_translation) generator of state wavefunctionals.

Schubert polynomials are generalizations of [Schur polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_polynomials) that represent cohomology classes of [Schubert cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_cycle)s in [flag varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_flag_variety).

Schwartz–Zippel lemma (also called the DeMillo–Lipton–Schwartz–Zippel lemma) is a tool commonly used in probabilistic [polynomial identity testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_identity_testing).

Schwinger model is a model describing 1+1D (time + 1 spatial dimension) [quantum electrodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_electrodynamics) (QED) which includes [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_equation), coupled to [photons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell's_equations).

Schwinger parametrization is a technique for evaluating [loop integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loop_integral)s which arise from [Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram)s with one or more loops.

Schwinger's quantum action principle is a [variational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variational_method) approach to [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics) and [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory).

Schwinger–Dyson equations (SDEs) or Dyson–Schwinger equations, named after [Julian Schwinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Schwinger) and [Freeman Dyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeman_Dyson), are general relations between [correlation functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_function_(quantum_field_theory)) in [quantum field theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) (QFTs).

secondary calculus is a proposed expansion of classical [differential calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_calculus) on [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s, to the [https://web.archive.org/web/20060928025421/http://diffiety.org/preprint/98/05_98abs.htm DIPS-05/98].

seesaw theorem, or seesaw principle, says roughly that a limit of trivial line bundles over [complete varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_variety) is a trivial line bundle.

Segal's Burnside ring conjecture, or, more briefly, the Segal conjecture, is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) in [homotopy theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_theory), a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics).
Segre classification is an algebraic classification of rank two [symmetric tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_tensor)s.

Segre embedding is a map used in [projective geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_geometry) to consider the [cartesian product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product) of two [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space)s as a [projective variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_variety).

Segre surface, studied by and , is an intersection of two [quadrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadric_surface) in 4-dimensional [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space).

Seidel adjacency matrix of a [simple undirected graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) G is a [symmetric matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_matrix) with a row and column for each vertex, having 0 on the diagonal, −1 for positions whose rows and columns correspond to adjacent vertices, and +1 for positions corresponding to non-adjacent vertices.

Seligmann Kantor (6 December 1857, [Sobědruhy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobědruhy) – 21 March 1903, Sobědruhy) was a [Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemia)n-born, German-speaking mathematician of [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews) origin in the [Austro-Hungarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Empire).

semi-local ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) for which R/J(R) is a [semisimple ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_ring), where J(R) is the [Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical) of R.

semi-locally simply connected (or semilocally simply connected) property is a certain [local connectedness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_connected_space) condition that arises in the theory of [covering space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space)s.

semi-orthogonal matrix is a non-[square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_matrix) [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) with [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) entries where: if the number of columns exceeds the number of rows, then the rows are [orthonormal vectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthonormal_vectors); but if the number of rows exceeds the number of columns, then the columns are orthonormal vectors.

semi-simplicity is a widespread concept in disciplines such as [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra), [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra), [representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory), [category theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory), and [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

semi-symmetric graph is an [undirected graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undirected_graph) that is [edge-transitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge-transitive_graph) and [regular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_graph), but not [vertex-transitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex-transitive_graph).

basic semialgebraic set is a set defined by polynomial equalities and polynomial inequalities, and a semialgebraic set is a [finite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_set) [union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(set_theory)) of basic semialgebraic sets.
semialgebraic space is a space which is locally [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) to a [semialgebraic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semialgebraic_set).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a subfield of [mathematical programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_programming) concerned with the optimization of a linear [objective function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objective_function) (a user-specified function that the user wants to minimize or maximize) over the intersection of the [cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_(linear_algebra)) of [[Positive-definite matrix#Negative-definite, semidefinite and indefinite matrices|positive semidefinite]] [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) with an [affine space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_space), i.e., a [spectrahedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrahedron).

semifield is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) with two [binary operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation)s, addition and multiplication, which is similar to a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)), but with some axioms relaxed.

[semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) with three elements is an object consisting of three elements and an [associative operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_operation) defined on them.

semigroup with two elements is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) for which the [cardinality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinality) of the [underlying set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underlying_set) is two.

semigroupoid (also called semicategory, naked category or precategory) is a [partial algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_algebra) that satisfies the axioms for a small [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)), except possibly for the requirement that there be an identity at each object.

join-semilattice (or upper semilattice) is a [partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set) that has a [join](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Join_(mathematics)) (a [least upper bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_upper_bound)) for any [nonempty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonempty_set) [finite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_set) [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset).

semiorthogonal decomposition is a way to divide a [triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category) into simpler pieces.

definition: semiprimitive ring or Jacobson semisimple ring or J-semisimple ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) whose [Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical) is [zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_ideal).
semiring is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure).

semisimple algebra is an [associative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) [Artinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artinian_ring) algebra over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) which has trivial [Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical) (only the zero element of the algebra is in the Jacobson radical).
semisimple if it is a [direct sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_sum_of_modules) of [simple Lie algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Lie_algebra).
semisimple module or completely reducible module is a type of module that can be understood easily from its parts.
separable algebra is a kind of [semisimple algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_algebra).

separable if its [roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_polynomial) are [distinct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinct_(mathematics)) in an [algebraic closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_closure) of K, that is, the number of distinct roots is equal to the [degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_a_polynomial) of the polynomial.

Sequential dynamical systems (SDSs) are a class of discrete [dynamical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_systems) and generalize many aspects of for example classical [cellular automata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellular_automata), and provide a framework for studying asynchronous processes over [graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_theory).
multisection of a power series is a new [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series) composed of equally spaced terms extracted unaltered from the original series.

Serre duality is a [duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_(mathematics)) for the [coherent sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf_cohomology) of algebraic varieties, proved by [Jean-Pierre Serre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Serre).

Serre group S is the pro-algebraic group whose [representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_representation) correspond to CM-motives over the [algebraic closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_closure) of the rationals, or to polarizable rational [Hodge structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_structure)s with abelian [Mumford–Tate group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumford–Tate_group)s.

Serre's multiplicity conjectures, named after [Jean-Pierre Serre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Serre), are certain problems in [commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra), motivated by the needs of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

sesquilinear form is a generalization of [inner product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product)s of [complex vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_vector_space)s, which are the most common sesquilinear forms.

setoid (X, ~) is a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) (or [type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_(mathematics))) X equipped with an [equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation) ~.

Severi–Brauer variety over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K is an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) V which becomes [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphic) to a [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) over an [algebraic closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_closure) of K.

sfermion is a hypothetical [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics))-0 [superpartner particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superpartner) (sparticle) of its associated [fermion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermion).

sgoldstino is any of the spin-0 [superpartner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superpartner)s of the [goldstino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstino) in [relativistic quantum field theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_quantum_field_theories) with [spontaneously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_symmetry_breaking) [broken supersymmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry_breaking).

sheaf (: sheaves) is a tool for systematically tracking data (such as [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics))s, [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group)s, [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics))s) attached to the [open set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set)s of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) and defined locally with regard to them.

sheaf cohomology is the application of [homological algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_algebra) to analyze the [global section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_section)s of a [sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_(mathematics)) on a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space).

presheaf of spectra on a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) X is a contravariant functor from the category of open subsets of X, where morphisms are inclusions, to the [good category of commutative ring spectra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_category_of_commutative_ring_spectra).

shear mapping is an [affine transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_transformation) that displaces each point in a fixed direction by an amount proportional to its [signed distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signed_distance_function) from a given [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_line) [parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_(geometry)) to that direction.

shelling of a [simplicial complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplicial_complex) is a way of gluing it together from its maximal simplices (simplices that are not a face of another simplex) in a well-behaved way.

Sherman–Takeda theorem states that if A is a [C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebra) then its double dual is a [W*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W*-algebra), and is isomorphic to the [weak closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_operator_topology) of A in the [universal representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_representation_(C*-algebra)) of A.

Shilov boundary is the smallest [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_set) subset of the [structure space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structure_space) of a [commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative) [Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra) where an analog of the [maximum modulus principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_modulus_principle) holds.

Shimura variety is a higher-dimensional analogue of a [modular curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_curve) that arises as a quotient [variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) of a [Hermitian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_symmetric_space) by a [congruence subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_subgroup) of a [reductive algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_group) defined over Q.

Springer resolution is a [resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities) of the variety of [nilpotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilpotent) elements in a [semisimple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra) [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra), .

spurion is a fictitious, auxiliary field in a [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) that can be used to parameterize any [symmetry breaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_breaking) and to determine all [operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_(physics))s invariant under the symmetry.

square-free element is an element r of a [unique factorization domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_factorization_domain) R that is not [divisible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain) by a non-trivial square.

square-free polynomial is a [univariate polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Univariate_polynomial) (over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) or an [integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain)) that has no [multiple root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_root) in an [algebraically closed field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraically_closed_field) containing its coefficients.

stability group of [subnormal series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_series) is the group of automorphisms that act as identity on each [quotient group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_group).
stabilizer code is a class of quantum [code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code)s for performing [quantum error correction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_error_correction).
stable group is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) that is stable in the sense of [stability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_theory).

stable principal bundle is a generalisation of the notion of a [stable vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_vector_bundle) to the setting of [principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)s.

stable vector bundle is a ([holomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_vector_bundle) or [algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_vector_bundle)) [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) that is stable in the sense of [geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory).
stably free module is a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) which is close to being [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_module).

stack or 2-sheaf is, roughly speaking, a [sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_(mathematics)) that takes values in [categories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) rather than sets.

staggered fermions (also known as Kogut–Susskind fermions) are a [fermion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermion) discretization that reduces the number of [fermion doublers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermion_doubling) from sixteen to four.

standard conjectures about algebraic cycles are several [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture)s describing the relationship of [algebraic cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycle)s and [Weil cohomology theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_cohomology_theory).

Stanley decomposition is a way of writing a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) in terms of polynomial subrings.

Stanley–Reisner ring, or face ring, is a quotient of a [polynomial algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_ring) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(algebra)) by a square-free [monomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomial_ideal) [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)).

statistical field theory (SFT) is a theoretical framework that describes systems with many degrees of freedom, particularly near [phase transitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transitions).

Steinberg representation, or Steinberg module or Steinberg character, denoted by St, is a particular [linear representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_representation) of a [reductive algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_algebraic_group) over a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field) or [local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field), or a group with a [BN-pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BN-pair).

definition: Steinitz exchange lemma is a theorem in [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra) concerning [bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_(linear_algebra)), [dimensionality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_(vector_space)) of a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space), stating that for any set smaller than a spanning set, there is a set of vectors in the spanning set but missing from the smaller set that can be added to the smaller set to make that set spanning as well.

stepwise irregular graph (or SI graph) is a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) in which the [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_(graph_theory)) of any two [adjacent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjacent_(graph_theory)) vertices differ by exactly one.
Steven Lawrence Kleiman (born March 31, 1942) is an American [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician).

Stieltjes matrix, named after [Thomas Joannes Stieltjes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Joannes_Stieltjes), is a [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_numbers) [symmetric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_matrix) [positive definite matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_definite_matrix) with [nonpositive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonpositive) [off-diagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-diagonal) entries.

Stokes operator, named after [George Gabriel Stokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gabriel_Stokes), is an unbounded [linear operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_operator) used in the theory of [partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation)s, specifically in the fields of [fluid dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics) and [electromagnetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetics).

straight-line program is, informally, a [program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_program) that does not contain any loop or any test, and is formed by a sequence of steps that apply each an [operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_(mathematics)) to previously computed elements.

string group is an infinite-dimensional group .

supersymmetry breaking or SUSY breaking is a process via which a seemingly non-[supersymmetric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetric) physics emerges from a supersymmetric theory.

topological combinatorics is the application of [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) and [algebro-topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) methods to solving problems in [combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics).
topological degree theory is a generalization of the [winding number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winding_number) of a curve in the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane).

topological half-exact functor F is a [functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functor) from a fixed topological [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) (for example [CW complexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CW_complexes) or [pointed space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointed_space)s) to an [abelian category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category) (most frequently in applications, category of [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group)s or category of [modules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) over a fixed ring) that has a following property: for each sequence of spaces, of the form: : X → Y → C(f) where C(f) denotes a [mapping cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapping_cone_(topology)), the sequence: : F(X) → F(Y) → F(C(f)) is [exact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exact_sequence).

topological modular forms (tmf) is the name of a [spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_(homotopy_theory)) that describes a generalized [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory).

topological module is a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(algebra)) over a [topological ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_ring) such that [scalar multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_multiplication) and addition are [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function_(topology)).

topological monoid is a [monoid object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoid_(category_theory)) in the [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) of [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s.

topological quantum field theory (or topological field theory or TQFT) is a [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) that computes [topological invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_invariant)s.

topological quantum number (also called topological charge) is any quantity, in a physical theory, that takes on only one of a discrete set of values, due to [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) considerations.
topological recursion is a recursive definition of invariants of spectral curves.
topological ring is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(algebra)) -adic fields]].

topological semigroup is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) that is simultaneously a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space), and whose semigroup operation is [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function).

Tor functors are the [derived functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derived_functor)s of the [tensor product of modules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product_of_modules) over a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)).

toral subalgebra is a [Lie subalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_subalgebra) of a general linear Lie algebra all of whose elements are [semisimple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_operator) (or [diagonalizable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonalizable_matrix) over an algebraically closed field).

Torelli theorem, named after [Ruggiero Torelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruggiero_Torelli), is a classical result of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) over the [complex number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number_field), stating that a [[Algebraic curve#Singularities|non-singular]] projective [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) ([compact Riemann surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Riemann_surface)) C is determined by its [Jacobian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_variety) J(C), when the latter is given in the form of a [principally polarized abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principally_polarized_abelian_variety).
toric ideal is an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) generated by differences of two [monomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomial)s.
toric stack is a [stacky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(mathematics)) generalization of a [toric variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toric_variety).

toric variety or torus embedding is a kind of [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) that contains an [algebraic torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_torus) whose [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) extends to the whole variety.
toroidal embedding is an open embedding of algebraic varieties that locally looks like the embedding of the open torus into a [toric variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toric_variety).

torsion element is an element of a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) that yields zero when multiplied by some [non-zero-divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-zero-divisor) of the [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)).

torsion abelian group is an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group) in which every [element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Element_(mathematics)) has [finite order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_order).

torsion-free abelian group is an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group) which has no non-trivial [torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torsion_(algebra)) elements; that is, a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) in which the [group operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_operation) is [commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_property) and the [identity element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_element) is the only element with finite [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(group_theory)).
torsor or a principal bundle is an analogue of a [principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle) in [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology).

torus action on an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) is a [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group-scheme_action) of an [algebraic torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_torus) on the variety.

trace field of a [linear group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_group) is the field generated by the [traces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_(linear_algebra)) of its elements.

trace is an [equivalence class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_class) of [string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_language)s, wherein certain letters in the string are allowed to [commute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_property), but others are not.

transgression map is a way to transfer [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology) classes.

triangle group is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) that can be realized geometrically by sequences of [reflections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflection_(mathematics)) across the sides of a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle).

triangular matrix is a special kind of [square matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_matrix).

triangular matrix ring, also called a triangular ring, is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) constructed from two rings and a [bimodule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bimodule).

triangulated category is a [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) with the additional structure of a The localizing subcategories of the whole stable homotopy category have not been classified.

definition: tridiagonal matrix algorithm, also known as the Thomas algorithm (named after [Llewellyn Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llewellyn_Thomas)), is a simplified form of [Gaussian elimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_elimination) that can be used to solve [tridiagonal systems of equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tridiagonal_matrix).
trinomial is a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) consisting of three terms or [monomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomial)s.
triple product is a product of three 3-[dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_(vector_space)) vectors, usually [Euclidean vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector)s.
trivial cylinders are certain [pseudoholomorphic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoholomorphic_curve)s appearing in certain cylindrical [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s.

trivial semigroup (a semigroup with one element) is a [semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup) for which the [cardinality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinality) of the [underlying set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underlying_set) is [one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One).

trope is an archaic term for a singular (meaning special) tangent space of a [variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety), often a [quartic surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartic_surface).

tropical compactification is a compactification ([projective completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_completion)) of a [subvariety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) of an [algebraic torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_torus), introduced by Jenia Tevelev.
TQBF is a [formal language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_language) consisting of the true quantified Boolean formulas.

truth table is a [mathematical table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_table) used in [logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic)—specifically in connection with [Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_(logic)), [Boolean function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_function)s, and [propositional calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propositional_calculus)—which sets out the functional values of logical [expressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expression_(mathematics)) on each of their functional arguments, that is, for each [combination of values taken by their logical variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_(logic)).

Tschirnhaus transformation, also known as Tschirnhausen transformation, is a type of mapping on [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s developed by [Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehrenfried_Walther_von_Tschirnhaus) in 1683.

Tsen rank of a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) describes conditions under which a system of [polynomial equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_equations) must have a solution in the [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)).

Tsen's theorem states that a function field K of an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) over an [algebraically closed field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraically_closed_field) is [quasi-algebraically closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-algebraically_closed) (i.e., C 1.

twisted cubic is a smooth, [rational curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_curve) C of [degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_an_algebraic_variety) three in [projective 3-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) P has the property that the tangent and secant lines are pairwise disjoint, except at points of the variety itself.

twisted mass fermions are a [fermion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermion) discretization that extends [Wilson fermions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_fermion) for two mass-degenerate fermions.

twisted Poincaré duality is a theorem removing the restriction on [Poincaré duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_duality) to [oriented manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriented_manifold)s.
twisted sector is a configuration of sectors in [orbifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbifold) [conformal field theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_field_theory).
twistor theory was proposed by [Roger Penrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Penrose) in 1967 * [http://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/lmason/Tn/ Twistor newsletter] archives.

two-dimensional conformal field theory is a [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) on a Euclidean [two-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_space), that is invariant under local [conformal transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_map)s.

definition: two-dimensional critical Ising model is the [critical limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_point_(thermodynamics)) of the [Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model) in two dimensions.

two-element Boolean algebra is the [Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_(structure)) whose underlying set (or [universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe_(mathematics)) or carrier) B is the [Boolean domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_domain).
two-graph is a set of unordered triples chosen from a finite vertex set X, such that every unordered quadruple from X contains an even number of triples of the two-graph.

type I supergravity is the theory of [supergravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergravity) in ten [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s with a single [supercharge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercharge).

type IIA supergravity is the unique [supergravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergravity) in ten [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s with two [supercharge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercharge)s of opposite [chirality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirality_(physics)).

type IIB supergravity is the unique [supergravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergravity) in ten [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s with two [supercharge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercharge)s of the same [chirality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirality_(physics)).

universal invariant or u-invariant of a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) describes the structure of [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form)s over the field.

Uehling potential describes the interaction potential between two electric charges which, in addition to the classical [Coulomb potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coulomb_potential), contains an extra term responsible for the electric [polarization of the vacuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_polarization).

ultragraph C*-algebra is a [universal C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_C*-algebra) generated by [partial isometries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_isometry) on a collection of [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space)s constructed from ultragraphs.
ultralimit is a geometric construction that assigns a limit [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space) to a sequence of metric spaces 115–197.

ultraviolet completion, or UV completion, of a [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) is the passing from a lower energy [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) to a more general quantum field theory above a threshold value known as the [cutoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutoff_(physics)).

ultraviolet divergence or UV divergence is a situation in which an [integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral), for example a [Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram), diverges because of contributions of objects with unbounded [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy), or, equivalently, because of physical phenomena at infinitesimal distances.

ultraweak topology, also called the weak-* topology, or weak-* operator topology or σ-weak topology, is a [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) on B(H), the space of [bounded operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_operator)s on a [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space) H.

unique factorization domain (UFD) (also sometimes called a factorial ring following the terminology of [Bourbaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Bourbaki)) is a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) in which a statement analogous to the [fundamental theorem of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_arithmetic) holds.

definition: unitary method is a problem-solving technique taught to students as a method for solving [word problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_(mathematics_education)) involving [proportionality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportionality_(mathematics)) and [units of measurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_of_measurement).

Universal algebra (sometimes called general algebra) is the field of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) that studies [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure)s in general, not specific types of algebraic structures.
universal C*-algebra is a [C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebra) described in terms of generators and relations.

universal embedding theorem, or Krasner–Kaloujnine universal embedding theorem, is a theorem from the mathematical discipline of [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory) first published in 1951 by [Marc Krasner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Krasner) and [Lev Kaluznin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lev_Kaluznin).

universal enveloping algebra of a [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) is the [unital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unital_algebra) [associative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) algebra whose [representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_representation) correspond precisely to the [representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_of_a_Lie_algebra) of that Lie algebra.

universal geometric algebra is a type of [geometric algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_algebra) generated by [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s endowed with an indefinite [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form).
universal quadratic form is a [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form) over a [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) that represents every element of the ring.

universal representation of a C*-algebra is a faithful representation which is the direct sum of the [[Gelfand–Naimark–Segal construction#The GNS construction|GNS representations]] corresponding to the states of the C*-algebra.
unramified morphism is a [morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphism_of_schemes) is zero.

Unruh–DeWitt detector is an idealized phenomenological model of a localized [quantum probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_measurement) used to operationalize the measurement of particles in curved or dynamical [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime)s.

winding number or winding index of a [closed curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_curve) in the [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)) around a given [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(mathematics)) is an [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) representing the total number of times that the curve travels counterclockwise around the point, i.e., the curve's [number of turns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_of_turns).

Witt algebra, named after [Ernst Witt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Witt), is the [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra) of meromorphic vector fields defined on the [Riemann sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_sphere) that are holomorphic except at two fixed points.

Witt vector is an [infinite sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_sequence) of elements of a [commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)).

Wold decomposition or Wold–von Neumann decomposition, named after [Herman Wold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Wold) and [John von Neumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_von_Neumann), is a [classification theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_theorem) for [isometric linear operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry)s on a given [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space).
word is any written product of [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) elements and their inverses.

word problem is the [problem of deciding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_problem) whether two given expressions are equivalent with respect to a set of [rewriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rewriting) identities.

[Wenjun Wu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu_Wenjun)'s method is an algorithm for solving [multivariate polynomial equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_of_polynomial_equations) introduced in the late 1970s by the Chinese [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) [Wen-Tsun Wu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu_Wenjun).
Wyckoff position is any point in a set of points whose site symmetry groups (see below) are all conjugate subgroups of one another.

Yukawa coupling or Yukawa interaction, named after [Hideki Yukawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Yukawa), is an interaction between particles according to the [Yukawa potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukawa_potential).

Yuri Tschinkel (Юрий Чинкель, born 31 May 1964 in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow)) is a Russian-German-American mathematician, specializing in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), [automorphic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphic_form)s and [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory).

Zariski ring is a commutative [Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) [topological ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_ring) A whose topology is defined by an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) is [faithfully flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faithfully_flat_module) over A (in general, it is only flat over A).

Zariski topology is a [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology_(structure)) defined on geometric objects called [varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety).
Zariski's connectedness theorem (due to [Oscar Zariski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Zariski)) says that under certain conditions the fibers of a morphism of varieties are connected.

Zariski's lemma, proved by , states that, if a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K is [finitely generated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_algebra) as an [associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra) over another field k, then K is a [finite field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field_extension) of k; that is, K is finitely generated as a [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) (in other words, K is a finite dimensional [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)) over k.

Zariski's main theorem, proved by , is a statement about the structure of [birational morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_morphism)s stating roughly that there is only one branch at any normal point of a [variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety).

zero-product property states that the product of two [nonzero elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_element) is nonzero.

zero-symmetric graph is a [connected graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connected_graph) in which each vertex has exactly three incident edges and, for each two vertices, there is a unique [symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_automorphism) taking one vertex to the other.
